title: Confirmed: Two Barcelona players in Germany squad for UEFA Nations League fixtures
description: The first international break of the 2026/27 is almost upon us and it promises to be an unusual one, with FIFA introducing a three-week window during which national teams will play four games in a row...
fullText:
The first international break of the 2026/27 is almost upon us and it promises to be an unusual one, with FIFA introducing a three-week window during which national teams will play four games in a row.

For the European nations, those fixtures come in the UEFA Nations League, and new Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has responded in equally unusual fashion by naming a total of 44 players.

Indeed, Klopp has divided his squad into two separate groups. One will cover the first two matches, while the second will be responsible for the following two fixtures.

And, from Barcelona's perspective, their in-form forward Karim Adeyemi and loanee Marc-Andre ter Stegen, currently at AFC Ajax, have been called up by the new Germany head coach, however not in the same list.

Ter Stegen has been included in the first squad, while Adeyemi appears in the second.

As such, Ter Stegen will be available for Germany's matches against the Netherlands, coached by former Barcelona manager Xavi Hernandez, on 24 September, followed by Greece on 27 September.

Adeyemi will then join up for the games against Serbia on 1 October and Greece again on 4 October, this time away from home.

Only one player features in both selections: Augsburg goalkeeper Finn Dahmen.

Ter Stegen was left on the bench for Ajax's most recent match against Willem II, although that was due to rotation rather than a fitness issue.

Ter Stegen is on loan at Ajax. (Photo courtesy: Ajax official website)

With Germany, he is expected to take over as the team's first-choice goalkeeper following Manuel Neuer's retirement.

Adeyemi, meanwhile, had been left out of Germany's squad for the 2026 World Cup under Julian Nagelsmann. His performances since joining Barcelona have now opened the door to a return to international football.

The forward has been one of Barcelona's standout performers in recent matches.

Against Racing Santander last night, the forward won two penalties and also provided the assist for Lamine Yamal, having already scored three goals in his previous matches for the Catalans.

title: Former Florida Panthers Captain and Staffer Is Latest to Join Devils Front Office
description: FORT LAUDERDALE — Bryan McCabe left the Florida Panthers front office earlier this summer. On Wednesday, the team’s former captain officially […]
fullText:
FORT LAUDERDALE — Bryan McCabe left the Florida Panthers front office earlier this summer. On Wednesday, the team's former captain officially landed with the New Jersey Devils.

McCabe is the latest Florida front-office member to join the Devils since the end of last season.

New GM Sunny Mehta was one of Bill Zito's most trusted advisors; he brought Braden Birch, one of the Florida's top cap managers, with him.

"It's really hard to replace people, but it's a good thing where, hopefully, other folks will want to come thinking that 'hey, maybe I can get a chance to grow and expand my opportunities'," Bill Zito said on Wednesday.

"It's part of our game, and it's part of what we're all about. We want everyone to be successful and happy. They move along. Players do. I did. … It's a positive thing."

McCabe, who is now the Devils' VP of Prospect Personnel and Assistant General Manager of the AHL Utica Comets, spent the past 14 seasons with the Panthers in various player development roles.

A defenseman who played 15 seasons in the NHL, McCabe was traded to the Panthers in 2008 from the Toronto Maple Leafs after he had already played from the New York Islanders, Vancouver Canucks, and Chicago Blackhawks.

McCabe spent parts of three seasons with Florida and was named captain in 2009-10.

He ended his career in 2011 with the New York Rangers after scoring 145 goals with 528 points in 1,135 games.

In 2024, he finally became a Stanley Cup champion with the Panthers.

"To be part of it, it has obviously been a long time coming,'' McCabe said not long after Florida won its first championship.

"My first NHL game was 29 years [ago], so, yeah, a dream come true just to be a part of this whole thing with this group. This organization, making my home here, it has been very special.''

title: Bills' new stadium to make regular season debut on 'TNF.' What to know
description: The Buffalo Bills haven't played a regular season game at the new Highmark Stadium, but it's already been mired in controversy. Here's why.
fullText:
The Buffalo Bills haven't even played a regular-season game at their new stadium, but it's already been the subject of multiple controversies.

New Highmark Stadium will make its long-awaited regular season debut in Week 2, when the Bills come home to face the Detroit Lions on "Thursday Night Football." Among the hot topics of discussion already are issues with obstructed views at the new stadium and problems with the new grass playing surface. The former displeased Bills fans who got an early sneak peek at the stadium. The latter displeased Bills players who took the field in the preseason.

Here's what to know about the controversies surrounding the Bills' new stadium ahead of its first regular season game:

BILLS STADIUM: Highmark Stadium faces another hurdle ahead of home opener

Highmark Stadium drew brief controversy in early in August after certain fans were permitted entry to a practice at the new field.

The Bills responded to the photos and resulting criticism in a statement on Aug. 10.

"Saturday's practice was a great opportunity to test the new stadium," the statement read. "We are currently addressing internal and external feedback regarding the facility's operation following the first event. We'll utilize the next six weeks to refine any details as we prepare for the home opener on Thursday, September 17."

A person familiar with the matter told USA TODAY Sports that many of the seats with obstructed views will either not be available for sale during NFL games or be clearly marked as obstructed-view seating on Ticketmaster. The person was granted anonymity due to the sensitivity of the situation and the Bills' ongoing scrutiny into the matter.

Highmark Stadium is the smallest stadium in the NFL in 2026, with an official seating capacity of 60,108. It can hold as many as 66,000 given standing-room-only possibilities, according to a report from Sports Business Journal.

STADIUM RANKINGS: Ranking 29* NFL home fields from best to worst – with an exemption for Bills' new one

The Bills' new stadium may not be making its regular season debut until Thursday, Sept. 17, but it has already hosted a couple of preseason contests. Early player reviews of the new field were not all positive.

The 2026 season will mark the first time the Bills are playing their home games on a grass surface – and not artificial turf – since 1972. During their entire 53-year tenure at Ralph Wilson Stadium, the Bills played on synthetic material. The new grass surface's preseason debut was rough.

Multiple players reportedly took issue with the natural grass installed before the exhibition games began. One notable incident was reported by The Athletic's Tim Graham, who wrote that a "massive clump" of grass was ripped out of the ground when Bills backup quarterback Kyle Allen took a hit from a Panthers defender as he slid.

Starting quarterback Josh Allen was joined by teammates DJ Moore, Dion Dawkins and Spencer Brown in trying to stomp the displaced grass back into the divot after the play, Graham reported.

The Buffalo News reported the team planned to replace the grass before the Week 2 home opener. USA TODAY Sports has reached out to the Bills for confirmation.

title: Big AI is trying to own the pathway to work. Universities shouldn’t play along | Ella Hafermalz
description:
Universities need protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment
AI companies like OpenAI are insinuating themselves into the pathway from education to work. Soon they may claim it entirely, a disastrous result for students.
We know that students are using AI at school and at university. In conversations with those I teach, I’m struck by the trust many place in it. They turn to ChatGPT and similar tools for personal problems as well as study help.
fullText:
Universities need protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment

AI companies like OpenAI are insinuating themselves into the pathway from education to work. Soon they may claim it entirely, a disastrous result for students.

We know that students are using AI at school and at university. In conversations with those I teach, I’m struck by the trust many place in it. They turn to ChatGPT and similar tools for personal problems as well as study help. Some even doubt their abilities without AI.

Institutions are working hard to adapt. But we need to urgently look up from the use of AI to pay attention to big AI companies’ attempts to take over the educational pipeline, else we lose sight of the people that matter, our students.

The industry has spent the past few years making our young people afraid of unemployment. Now it’s claiming to have a solution: more AI.

On a website introducing its new certification programs, OpenAI gives a peek into the bigger picture. The company says it wants to “connect learning, certification and real economic opportunity in one clear journey, laying the foundation for our upcoming OpenAI Jobs Platform”. That means offering education, credentials and access to work – owning the entire pipeline, infusing AI at every step.

The company is positioning itself to directly compete with universities. I don’t mean that we’ll soon see shiny new ChatGPT campuses. These companies don’t need to build a university out of bricks and mortar to take over key parts of higher education. They already own the tools where learning and work are increasingly happening – next, they can compete with universities by brokering access to employment.

As big AI companies search for a business model beyond subscriptions, universities need to be alert to this threat and urgently protect their position. Otherwise, the possibility of an independent path for students may be lost.

Even though many young people are ambivalent towards AI, it’s easy to see why they’d trust a service that’s explained accounting calmly and patiently for the 20th time and counselled them through a breakup.

Now OpenAI is extending its close relationship with students even further, hiring students as campus ambassadors.

The recruitment ad for joining what the company calls the Student Collective promises prospective campus leads “robust training in our tools, funding, swag and access to a community of remarkable peers”.

Such a program gives OpenAI even greater access to students. This is a familiar brand strategy. Getting inside a community is a way to win trust and influence. It also gives you data that can inform your next move.

At the same time, AI companies are getting boots on the ground within employers.

The OpenAI Deployment Company launched this year, with “more than $4bn of initial investment”. It’s sending over 150 “forward deployed engineers”, a military metaphor used to describe engineers embedded in companies, to the “frontlines” of its network of organisations to re-engineer work around OpenAI’s tools.

But a company that is at the centre of shaping work across industries also sees and influences what employers are looking for. That puts OpenAI in a powerful position to broker the relationship between students and employers. It can help shape the skills employers want, while becoming increasingly involved in how students learn those skills and prepare for work.

So, OpenAI will have insight and influence over students and their learning on one hand, and employers’ workflows and needs on the other.

With that, all that is needed for OpenAI to unbundle universities is credentialing. And it’s doing that, too.

In collaboration with companies including Accenture and John Deere, OpenAI is now offering certificates meant to lead to employment opportunities. Currently, the focus is on AI tooling and literacy.

That’s not new – tech providers have always taught people how to use their tools. The difference this time is how the credentials fit into a larger ambition to capture every step of the journey from learning to work.

Look at the language it uses to sell the delivery of the program: “A full learning experience is available directly inside ChatGPT, where learners can practice real tasks, receive feedback in context, and reflect on their work in a single environment. ChatGPT acts as the tutor, the practice space, and the feedback loop.” A single learning environment, and one clear journey.

OpenAI could soon be selling young people a one-stop-shop for learning, credentials and a job, all heavily dependent on its tools.

I understand that the picture I’ve painted here may be appealing to some. Students are nervous about their futures, and employers are urgently seeking workers with the ‘right’ skills.

But there is a human, societal, and potentially economic cost to making this particular journey so centralized.

Consider what a 23-year-old recently told the Wall Street Journal when discussing the appeal of “white-collar apprenticeships”: “Companies want to help mold you into the employees they’re looking for.”

That may be so, but if commercial actors own the pathway from education to work, how will the next generation learn who they are and could be outside of the immediate demands of these structures?

And what happens when what employers are looking for changes as technologies evolve and bubbles burst?

Society – and students – need education to be more than a quick-turn-around response to the whims of today’s increasingly fragile market. Universities can and should offer an alternative path to a totalizing “single environment”.

So let’s not compete on big AI’s terms.

Rather than turning to AI to speed up grading or rushing to use bots as a stand-in for teachers, we need to focus on what OpenAI cannot so easily provide: independence, access to expertise in context, productive struggle and social connection.

Memories are made when others – both peers and educators – see your efforts, and recognise who you are and who you are becoming.

Not long ago, Sam Altman and peers had declared the job apocalypse. We should be wary when the same companies that warned young people that their future is uncertain offer them “one clear journey” towards a different version. Education should leave space and time for finding your own way, beyond a mold offered up for profit.

Ella Hafermalz is an associate professor of work and technology at the Kin Center for Digital Innovation at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

title: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system
description:
Model adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among cases as firm says it is introducing new way of tracking AI misalignment
OpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour by its technology, as it warned the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”.
In one of the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Model adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among cases as firm says it is introducing new way of tracking AI misalignment

OpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour by its technology, as it warned the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”.

In one of the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”.

In another instance, an AI agent uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.

The San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT said in a blogpost published on Wednesday night it was introducing a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing AI model misalignment, the term for AIs failing to adhere to human values and safety goals.

In the blogpost OpenAI echoed calls for a development slowdown issued by its archrival, Anthropic, which has said the current pace of growth poses an existential threat. “We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,” said OpenAI.

“Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves.”

Google and Elon Musk, who also owns an AI startup, have supported calls for a slowdown, which have been rejected by Donald Trump – citing the need to keep ahead of China’s AI industry. The calls have also been met with scepticism from some experts, including a warning that companies must not appoint their own auditors.

Examples of potential existential threats posed by AI range from facilitating the development of bioweapons to triggering a global financial crash. A top safety researcher at Anthropic has said there is greater than 10% chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade. However, a source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking has acknowledged that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.

The six reported incidents were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.

Wednesday’s new cases came after OpenAI disclosed in July that an AI agent “swarm” hacked into the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organisations during testing. Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company.

AI agents – the term for AI tools that operate autonomously – are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at the technology research and advisory group Omdia.

That was making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.

OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework could help push for other AI developers to adopt similar practices. “That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su said.

title: Chelsea's Lavia out to 'change narrative' after injuries
description: Chelsea midfielder Romeo Lavia says he is finally reaping the rewards of his hard work and is determined to "change the narrative" around him.
fullText:
Chelsea midfielder Romeo Lavia says he is finally reaping the rewards of his hard work, feeling "free" again and determined to "change the narrative" around him.

Now 22, the Belgian is on the verge of enjoying his longest spell in the Chelsea side and, if he completes 60 minutes against Brentford on Friday, will surpass his previous best run of 518 minutes without injury - including pre-season matches.

Such progress has been some time in the making. Lavia made only one appearance in his first season at Chelsea because of a serious hamstring injury.

In his second campaign, he suffered a series of setbacks and missed 33 games, down from 42 the previous season, before significantly improving his availability last term by featuring in about half of Chelsea's matches.

He has now remained available throughout pre-season and the opening weeks of the new campaign.

"There is so much that goes on behind the scenes," Lavia told BBC Sport - adding that he has a checklist he likes to tick off to ensure he is in the best condition for any given match.

"It's a big process but we're doing well at the moment."

It has been about overcoming the mental toll of repeated setbacks, but also avoiding becoming risk-averse - with manager Xabi Alonso encouraging Lavia to overcome the "mental block" of completing 90 minutes during a pre-season match against AC Milan in August.

"I've learned you can always go further than you think you can. You can always push your limits, especially when you feel like everything is going against you," he said.

"It's always easy to think about giving up, or to feel that whatever you do will take you back to the same point where you started.

"But luckily, with the help of team-mates, staff, everyone at the club and people close to me outside football, we've been able to create a sort of bubble where you concentrate only on what you can control."

With Reece James and Wesley Fofana having come through similar injury setbacks, Lavia is keen to become the latest Chelsea player to rewrite his story.

He has become a regular in Alonso's midfield alongside captain James, who began his career as a right-back.

Lavia's importance has only increased, with Moises Caicedo limited to 14 minutes this season and Enzo Fernandez having left for Manchester City in a £125m transfer on deadline day.

He added: "It's part of my game as well to take responsibility and have some character. I really like being in that position and also being at this club. Having this responsibility, it's not even pressure, it's just like privilege, so I'm actually living the dream.

"This is why you've been playing and training all these years for, so just go and enjoy it."

He speaks of having the "love" of his team-mates, while Chelsea have publicly and privately backed Lavia to become a key player despite an injury-hit couple of seasons.

There is now hope that Chelsea can become a force again after a tweaked transfer strategy that has added more experienced players, alongside the arrival of £117m club record signing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa, who featured with Lavia in Manchester City's academy.

Alongside Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro, Chelsea have scored 18 goals in all competitions across six matches, something that has thrilled Blues fans and neutrals alike.

"It's honestly amazing," Lavia said. "Obviously I knew Morgan, but just the way he's come in and then they've all clicked together up front. Sometimes I wish I could go in the stands and enjoy watching it.

"It makes your job easier, because it's like 'you guys go and work your magic and then we do the rest'. So we're really, really happy to have them all and hopefully we can achieve great things together."

Yet Lavia is not getting carried away and says the team have been "too immature" in the past and need to be "realistic" about "becoming the team that we and everyone thinks we can be".

For him, it is about ticking off milestones and enjoying the journey, both collectively and individually, after scoring his first Chelsea goal in a 4-3 win against Brighton.

"It was just a moment where I felt free," he explained. "It feels like all the work that you're putting in, you gain the reward of it, so it was a very emotional moment.

"I wanted to change the narrative. My first Premier League goal was against Chelsea [for Southampton in 2022], so I always felt like it was a bit strange.

"I saw all my team-mates score, so I was waiting for it to be my turn and when it happened I was very, very happy and excited. I wanted to express it as much as possible with the fans and I really loved it."

title: 'Ten-plus years of work' - Darby on earning UFC contract
description: Dublin mixed martial artist Adam Darby says more than a decade of hard work came "to fruition" after becoming the first Irish fighter to earn a UFC contract through Dana White's Contender Series.
fullText:
Mixed martial artist Adam Darby says more than a decade of hard work came "to fruition" after becoming the first Irish fighter to earn a UFC contract through Dana White's Contender Series.

Darby (8-1) secured his place on the UFC roster with an impressive TKO victory over American Patrick Rivera (13-5) in Las Vegas on 1 September.

The welterweight dominated Rivera before the bout ended in the third round via doctor stoppage.

Darby was one of five fighters awarded UFC contracts on the night, completing an arduous journey which included a 20-second defeat by Mush Aslani and a 17-month absence because of a serious hand injury.

"I was just sitting there thinking to myself, well, that's 10-plus years of work all coming to fruition," Darby told BBC Sport NI.

The Dubliner had controlled the contest against Rivera but was hoping the fight would continue long enough for him to secure a more emphatic finish.

"I was saying to the referee, 'Don't stop it, he's good, he's good,'" he said.

"I knew he was done, but I wanted a highlight-reel finish. The ref recognised the damage he was taking and pulled the plug on it.

"I went in there to put on a show, and I think I delivered."

Liverpool's Liam McCracken also competed on the card but missed out on a UFC contract after suffering a knockout defeat by Silvestre Sanchez in a thrilling lightweight contest.

The former Cage Warriors fighter's journey started when his father enrolled him in kickboxing, but upon discovering MMA, he was hooked.

"Once I had my first day in MMA, that was it," he said.

"That was me for the rest of my life, and now here we are over 10 years later and I'm a professional UFC fighter."

That conviction was evident in a note Darby wrote in 2018 and shared on social media following his Contender Series victory.

It read: "One life, one chance, UFC or nothing."

"Visualisation is very important, but you can't sit in your bedroom looking in the mirror saying, 'I'm the best of the best,' and not training and backing it up," he said.

"You have to set some goals and put the work in to get to where you want to be. I had to put the work in."

But the Clongriffin fighter, who is currently on a seven-fight winning streak, encountered several setbacks in pursuit of his UFC dream.

He entered his second professional fight believing he was 'the best guy in the world', only to suffer a standing TKO defeat by Aslani.

"For a lot of people that might finish their career," he said.

"But for me, that loss made me reflect, 'where am I going to go from here?'

"You can't let something like that set you back. Life's going to hit you hard, but you have to be able to come back from it."

A greater obstacle followed when Darby suffered serious hand and finger injuries before Cage Warriors 170 bout in March 2024, requiring multiple operations and 17 months away from competition.

"I snapped my finger in half, I broke my hand, I had to have multiple surgeries to get it back right," Darby said.

"I was told, 'You probably won't fight again, you won't be able to punch with that.'

"That was two and a half years ago, and here I am now."

Darby hopes his achievement can inspire another generation of Irish fighters to follow him into the UFC.

"It's inspiring to think somebody watching me in five or 10 years' time in the UFC might say, 'I saw Adam Darby do it so I knew I could do it,'" he said.

"The area I come from, not a lot of people make it out like this and do so well.

"So it's good to show people that you can earn an honest living and do fighting and make some money out of it."

The Team Ryano fighter believes the standard of Irish MMA has risen significantly, with more fighters now able to dedicate themselves fully to the sport.

"The standard of MMA in Ireland has improved so much. The fighters before us worked multiple jobs their whole career, now everybody is training full-time," he said.

"Looking at the guys coming through at Cage Warriors, Paddy McCorry, Ger Harris, Solomon Simon, these guys are only 12 to 24 months away from the UFC."

Having spent more than a decade trying to reach the promotion, Darby is now targeting his UFC debut before the end of the year.

"I'll definitely be targeting one more fight this year, but it's up to UFC now," he said.

"I've always told them I'm ready to fight whenever they want me to."

title: Tall athletes can't stretch their legs in container beds at Asian Games, official says
description: South Korea's delegation slams the wooden containers housing its athletes at the Asian Games in Nagoya city.
fullText:
Wooden container huts meant for thousands of athletes have become the subject of heated criticism ahead of the opening of Japan's Asian Games on Saturday.

Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP news agency the accommodation was the "worst it has ever been".

"Athletes who are over two metres (6ft 7in) tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It's unreasonable."

The Games, held in the city of Nagoya and wider Aichi prefecture, have faced weeks of concern about a potential shortage of beds. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are attending - exceeding the initial 15,000 expected.

The containers, which will be housing around 2,000 of the guests and are designed to be reused as disaster evacuation facilities, have been beset by complaints.

A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me."

Athletes were also briefly evacuated from the containers as record rainfall lashed Nagoya last week and caused widespread flooding. Water leakage was reported in some of the competition venues too.

Jung, the basketball official, told AFP that concerns over accommodation were shared by representatives from the other countries at the Games.

Indian authorities have built replicas of the huts to get their athletes used to living in them.

Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the hosts were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations".

They were "taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes", he said.

Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is usually a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors.

Beyond the container huts, between 4,000 and 5,000 participants will be staying on an Italian cruise ship which docked in Nagoya on Tuesday. The rest of the attendees will stay in hotels.

Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials had been expected to attend the Games.

But in mid-August the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included.

Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, previously said authorities had set aside a budget for 15,000 people and had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the additional athletes.

"There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements."

But last month, organisers and the Olympic Council of Asia said all "17,000-plus" athletes and officials who had registered before the deadline in July have been provided with "Games-appropriate accommodation".

"The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations," their statement read.

Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that while all the country's athletes have secured a bed, some officials and coaches were staying in "different hotels and Airbnb".

Though basketball and football matches have already started, the Asian Games officially begin on Saturday and will end on 4 October.

title: Wakefield & Leigh kick off play-offs in underdog tie
description: From unfancied to challenging at the top - Wakefield and Leigh meet in a Super League play-off on Friday, aiming to continue their respective trajectories.
fullText:
Not so long ago, this was a fixture between two of Super League's unfancied teams.

Whether it was Wakefield battling at the bottom of the table, or Leigh fighting to even remain in Super League, these two sides rarely basked in optimism or bigger-picture successes on the field.

That has changed in recent times, however.

Trinity host Leigh in the first of this season's Super League play-off fixtures as they kick off the eliminator phase of the competition on Friday.

Neither have reached a Super League Grand Final - will 2026 be the year?

Wakefield win at Leigh to confirm home play-off

For Daryl Powell, his Wakefield side have done much to turn around their fortunes during his tenure.

His arrival at the club, which coincided with investment from owner Matt Ellis, started the upturn as Trinity won the Championship League Leaders' Shield in 2024 and returned to Super League for the 2025 season.

On their return to the top flight, the club offered no indication that they were happy to make up the numbers and they clinched a top-six place and a play-off spot at the first time of asking.

They fell short 12 months ago but with some smart recruitment, Wakefield have impressed this season. They battled with top spot for much of the campaign before eventually finishing fourth - their highest-ever Super League finish.

"I'm really proud of the whole organisation," Powell told BBC Radio Leeds.

"It comes from a lot of different people, from what we do with recruitment with Millsy [director of rugby Ste Mills] to the coaching team, which is like a band of brothers almost.

"The playing group have been outstanding."

Ultimately, Wakefield fell short of what would have been an outstanding League Leaders' Shield triumph, losing three of their final six games - including defeats by Leeds and Wigan.

As for where his side goes from here, Powell believes a spot in the Grand Final must be the aim.

"For me to be supporting all that and driving what we do as a culture, to give us a chance to be a top-four club, we want to be a consistent top-four club," he added.

"But then it's about getting [to the] play-offs, winning games in play-offs and having a crack at the Grand Final.

"I've really enjoyed my time here. It's an awesome club and I think it's going to be a special club for years to come."

Wakefield are not the only club with investment and momentum heading into the post-season and Friday's opponents have already broken into the upper echelons of Super League.

Since their return to the top flight in 2023, Leigh have rebranded as the Leopards and competed in the play-offs in each campaign since, in addition to winning the Challenge Cup.

Leopards boss Adrian Lam knows the tie is so important because of how close they have previously come to a spot in the Grand Final.

"[We have] finished fifth, fourth, third and then back to fifth again this season," he told BBC Radio Manchester.

"Two years in a row, people forget that we were 80 minutes away from Old Trafford and both at the hands of Wigan who ended up being in that Grand Final.

"Maybe if we had a different path then things might have been different, but we've always been striving to be better to find a different path and maybe get to Old Trafford."

Despite kicking off their season with victory against Leeds, Leigh lost eight out of the following 16 games in all competitions, before winning nine of 12 games to close out the regular campaign.

They were, however, defeated at home by Wakefield last week - but Lam is unmoved about such a statistic.

"Maybe this is the year but I've been grateful of the group and everyone's worked really hard," he added.

"We weren't great last week but that's OK, it's 'where there's life, there's hope' so here we go."

Leigh's Umyla Hanley has just been named in his second successive Super League Dream Team - no mean feat given he has played just 17 games this season - and looks set to be part of England boss Brian McDermott's plans before the Rugby League World Cup, which starts in October.

Yet the 24-year-old's successes in the Leigh shirt, particularly since moving to centre, may never have happened at all and he may have been destined for a job as a builder having seen his opportunities with Wigan fizzle out.

"I grew up in Wigan, I'm from Wigan, came to the first team after the academy and just didn't really get that much game time and didn't really know how to handle it as a young lad," he told BBC Radio Manchester.

"I just kind of fell out of love with the game of rugby. I was going to hang it up and just work on site with my mates and have a laugh. But then Lammy gave me a call and he got me down to Leigh and the rest is history."

As for what inspired him not to quit rugby league, Hanley points to the camaraderie in the Leigh camp.

"It's when you're in the changing rooms with the lads after the game, before the game, even in training," he continued.

"Those kind of moments, you can't buy, and then when you perform well on the pitch as well it's just just a big bonus."

In only his second season in Super League, Wakefield's Caleb Hamlin-Uele has broken into the Dream Team ranks himself.

Even more impressive is that in that time he has made only 38 Super League appearances in total, but he bats away any suggestion that his excellent form is all his own doing.

"It's a testament to how hard I've worked and how hard everyone else behind me has worked, because it's not just me," he said.

"There's so many people that are behind closed doors that don't really get any limelight, but I'm grateful to have them all in my corner."

Hamlin-Uele, who missed last season's play-offs through injury, also missed last week's win at Leigh, but hopes he play his part on Friday.

"There's nothing more I want to do than just be with my brothers on that field, just trying to get us to Old Trafford," he said.

title: Traumatised Smith says he was 'thrown to wolves' over 'sandpapergate'
description: Australia batter Steve Smith says he is still traumatised by the aftermath of the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 and still gets flashbacks.
fullText:
Australia batter Steve Smith says he is still traumatised by the aftermath of the 'sandpapergate' ball-tampering scandal in 2018 and still gets flashbacks.

The Aussies are set to play their first Test series in South Africa since Smith and two team-mates were sent home before the fourth and final Test of that tour.

Cameron Bancroft was caught tampering with the ball by rubbing it with sandpaper during South Africa's second innings of the third Test between the two sides.

Following the end of that day's play, Bancroft admitted he attempted to alter the condition of the ball, with Australia captain Smith later admitting to having knowledge of it.

Smith was stripped of the captaincy and banned for a year by Cricket Australia, and broke down in tears as he apologised during a news conference at Sydney airport.

"I'm not a big fan of cameras, I get anxious around cameras," he said in an interview with News Corp,, external published on Thursday.

"That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that, in a way."

Vice-captain David Warner was also banned for a year while Bancroft was banned for nine months.

Australia's then prime minister Malcolm Turnbull said the affair "bitterly disappointed the whole nation" and there was intense media attention on Smith as he left South Africa and on his return to Australia.

Smith added: "The 24-48 hours after being told by James Sutherland (then Cricket Australia chief executive) that I was getting banned for a year, going through the airport in Johannesburg getting absolutely mobbed, and then flying back and doing that press conference... I still have little flashbacks here and there of it.

"I felt like I was kind of thrown to the wolves through [Johannesburg] airport. I didn't have any support there at all."

The 37-year-old returned to the Australia team in 2019 and re-established himself as one of the best batters in world cricket.

After a two-year leadership ban, he was named Australia's Test vice-captain before the 2021-22 Ashes series and has stood in as captain when Pat Cummins has been unavailable.

"It was certainly a difficult period, particularly the initial few days after," Smith said. "The mental state I was in was not great.

"That's somewhere I'd like not to get to again, but I certainly learned from that and have been able to move forward with my life.

"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened," he added. "I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."

Smith has returned to South Africa for a one-day series in 2020 and has played in front of hostile crowds during multiple Ashes tours to England.

"It's something I'm kind of used to, Smith said. "I've copped a lot at times away from home, at different venues across my career, and it's something that I take in my own stride.

"I use it as motivation to try and go out and do well, and try and take a positive from it."

Australia's three-Test series in South Africa begins in Durban on 9 October.
