title: Do Celtic have 'big issues', or will next four days hush concerns?
description: Chris Sutton believes his former side have "great concerns" despite a winning start to the Scottish Premiership season. The next four days will tell us whether those worries are justified.
fullText:
Football in Glasgow's goldfish bowl has a habit of being unnecessarily dramatised, yet there is a case for saying a week in mid-September could have a defining impact on Celtic's season.

After spectacularly failing the first of three tests during this mini crucial spell, alarm bells are ringing among sections of an unconvinced support.

Martin O'Neill's side have the chance to right the wrongs of their sobering 3-0 Premier Sports Cup quarter-final defeat by Rangers at Ibrox when they host their city rivals in a rematch in the league on Sunday, but a Europa League opener with Ferencvaros comes first.

Celtic fans are tiptoeing with trepidation into their first European action since their Champions League play-off collapse in Linz, a capitulation that has the same supporters questioning this team's big-game credentials, especially after Sunday.

"It's strange you're never asked about team selection when you win games," O'Neill responded bullishly when asked about the outside noise.

"We've been doing a fair amount of winning domestically now for quite some considerable time and we've won our league games so far.

"It's another big test for us on Sunday, obviously, but it's amazing the number of times you're not questioned when you've won."

McGregor laments Celtic's 'team of individuals'

Celtic & Scotland legend McGrain diagnosed with Alzheimer's

Visit our Celtic page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

In short: the aforementioned big-game results this season and the performance level under O'Neill since January.

The 74-year-old's remit last term was to end a chaotic, rollercoaster campaign on a high after the Wilfried Nancy debacle. He absolutely did that, winning the Scottish Premiership title and Scottish Cup.

Celtic fans spent the aftermath of that double triumph torn over whether they wanted to watch their legendary manager head off into the sunset with two medals round his neck or have him lead the team into a fresh season. Even O'Neill was unsure.

One thing supporters were united on, though, was wanting to see overdue progress in Europe and a better product on the pitch. It seems they are still waiting for that.

Europa League: Celtic v Ferencvaros

Thursday, 16 September (20:00 BST)

Listen to live match commentary on BBC Sounds and follow text updates on the BBC Sport website and app.

There will be fans of rival clubs who will view those wishes as greed, given Celtic still continue to dominate domestically.

However, supporters of the Parkhead side have spent the past decade being conditioned into watching their team clean up trophies while still delivering dominant, free-flowing football, hence the demand is there.

O'Neill and his staff were largely given a pass last term during a season of intense turbulence. Fury was mostly directed towards the club's hierarchy, but the manager and his backroom team are now not immune from scrutiny.

The Celtic boss's team selection has been questioned by fans and pundits, including one of his former players, Chris Sutton, in the wake of an abject derby display.

Below-par showings were forgiven last season as Celtic simply just had to get by to stay in touch at the top before eventually leapfrogging Heart of Midlothian on the final day with a seventh successive league victory.

That Premiership-winning streak has been extended to 13 games following six straight victories to start the campaign, but concerns about performance level remain. Four of those six wins have been by a one-goal margin.

Twelve goals over three wins at Kilmarnock, Dundee United and in the first leg of the Champions League play-off against LASK sent an ominous warning to Celtic's domestic rivals amid a period of high spending, particularly in forward areas.

Camilo Duran has been the standout summer recruit so far with six goals and three assists in 10 appearances, while record signing Kasper Hogh and fellow big-money arrival Haissem Hassan are yet to fully settle.

Sutton said his old club have been "flat-track bullies" by "beating the teams you expect them to beat", but the collapse in Austria, plus Sunday's bruising loss, has highlighted glaring deficiencies.

Even captain Callum McGregor lamented Celtic's "team of individuals" after the weekend defeat at Ibrox.

Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club, former striker Sutton also expressed his "great concerns" for O'Neill's men and said they have "big issues" after a "lightweight" midfield was "run all over" by Rangers.

Celtic have struggled to build up play against coherent pressing teams, which results in opposition sides being offered too much encouragement when the ball turns over.

They faced a whopping 60 shots across both legs with LASK. Forty of them came in a mess of a second leg. In the Premiership alone this season, they have faced 64 attempts, the same number as Hearts and six more than Rangers.

Over just six games, that tally already makes up almost a quarter of the total they faced in the entirety of the 2024-25 league-winning campaign under Brendan Rodgers.

That said, in comparison to last term, which was overseen by Rodgers, Nancy and O'Neill, Celtic's Premiership numbers show they are currently averaging a far better goal concession rate while scoring and shooting more.

Come Sunday, though, the most crucial statistic could be in the points column.

With a rapid rematch against Rangers offering the chance to move eight points clear of their city rivals after a test against European-level opposition, the next four days will at least be mood-shifting.

Whether that is to O'Neill's benefit remains unclear.

title: How an Aston Villa fringe player became Europe's most prolific scorer
description: No player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals than Donyell Malen since his Roma debut in January - BBC Sport examines his transformation.
fullText:
Just eight months ago, Donyell Malen was struggling to make a significant impact at Aston Villa.

Today, no player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals since his Roma debut on 18 January.

The Netherlands international has enjoyed a remarkable turnaround since joining Roma, transforming from a player who struggled to establish himself in the Premier League into one of the continent's most productive forwards.

Since his Roma debut, Malen has scored 20 goals, more than Harry Kane (16), Lamine Yamal (15) and anyone else in the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 during the same period.

He also leads the way for combined goals and assists with 22, ahead of Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes (20), Barcelona's teenage sensation Lamine Yamal (19) and Bayern striker Kane (18).

No player across Europe's top five leagues has made a greater contribution in front of goal.

The contrast with his time at Villa could hardly be greater.

In 46 appearances for the Premier League club, the 27-year-old scored 10 goals and registered two assists. Since joining Roma, he has scored 21 goals and provided three assists in just 25 matches.

His scoring rate has improved from one goal every 149.8 minutes at Villa to one every 96.7 minutes in Rome.

On the surface, the figures suggest two very different versions of the same player. But Roma's success with Malen may owe as much to how he is being used as to any change in confidence or form.

The Dutchman arrived in Italy with a proven goalscoring pedigree and the data suggests Roma have found a role that maximises his attacking instincts.

While confidence and form may have played a part, a change in position appears to be a major factor behind the resurgence.

At Villa, Malen was often used across the frontline and spent only 52% of his league minutes as a central striker. At Roma, 99% of his Serie A minutes have come through the middle under manager Gian Piero Gasperini, making him the focal point of the attack and placing him where he can do the most damage.

The stats are backed up by the eye test. After Roma's 1-1 Champions League draw with Fenerbahce last Thursday, when Malen set up his side's goal, French football journalist Julien Laurens told Match of the Day the Dutchman had become central to Gasperini's plans.

"He has been incredible since January," said Laurens.

"He has been really efficient, super clinical. Malen is at the heart of everything they do with the ball."

Malen is not the only former Premier League player to have flourished in Italy.

Former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay has thrived since swapping Old Trafford for Naples. Since joining Napoli in August 2024, only five players have scored more Serie A goals than the Scotland international's 22.

His impact has been such that Napoli supporters have even erected a street shrine in his honour.

Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund has also enjoyed an upturn in fortunes. His time in north west England divided opinion among supporters and pundits alike.

But since his Napoli debut, only Federico Dimarco, Lautaro Martinez and Malen have recorded more goal involvements than the Denmark international (19).

Their success highlights how a move to Serie A can provide players with the opportunity to thrive in a different environment and role.

For Malen, however, the transformation has been particularly dramatic.

Rather than changing Malen's game, Roma appear to have found a role that gets the best out of him. Used almost exclusively as a striker, the Dutchman has responded by producing the kind of form that first brought him to the attention of Europe's biggest clubs.

For a player whose Premier League spell failed to meet expectations, his resurgence in Italy's capital ranks among the most notable revivals in European football this year.

title: How history-making Classic success helped jockey shed fear of failure
description: St Leger-winning jockey Saffie Osborne says the "fear of failure" has left her now she has won a British Classic, becoming the first woman to do so.
fullText:
St Leger-winning jockey Saffie Osborne says the "fear of failure" has left her after she became the first woman to win a British Classic.

The 24-year-old said that despite wanting to achieve "so much more", her victory at Doncaster on Saturday means she will always be able to look back and think her career was "worth it".

Osborne said the sport can be "very lonely" - she estimates she drives 65,000 miles a year, often alone - and she has suffered some serious falls, breaking numerous bones.

But she told BBC Sport that winning one of British Flat racing's five Classics had been a dream since she was five. She has now fulfilled it.

While racing is a sport where men and women compete against one another, opportunities have not been equal.

Only six female jockeys have had rides in British Classics in 250 years, totalling 12 rides, according to the National Horseracing Museum.

They are Gay Kelleway (The Oaks, 1986; The Oaks, 1987), Alex Greaves (The Derby, 1996; 1,000 Guineas, 1996), Hayley Turner (The Derby, 2012) Josephine Gordon (1,000 Guineas, 2017), Hollie Doyle (The Oaks, 2021; St Leger, 2021; The Oaks, 2022) and Saffie Osborne (2,000 Guineas, 2024; 1,000 Guineas, 2026; St Leger, 2026).

"It has been a male-dominated sport for an extremely long time, and I suppose it's becoming less and less of a conversation, which is quite nice," she said.

"When people talk about the firsts of what women have done, I think to have my own one is quite special.

"I think it's also quite poignant because there's so few left of first things for women to do in this sport."

On Saturday's groundbreaking win, she added: "That sort of fear of failure has sort of disappeared. However much more I want to achieve, and I want to achieve so much more, it's kind of like I can always look back on my career and know that it was all worth it.

"I got to achieve what I always dreamed of achieving."

Osborne's ride on Highwayman in the St Leger was her first for trainer Joseph O'Brien, and only came about because of an injury to regular jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle.

She acknowledged that the success of a jockey is dependent on "being chosen", but is adamant that her gender isn't a factor in the opportunities she gets.

"I don't feel like in my position now that I'm ever looked at any differently because I'm a woman," she said.

"Any jockey, when you're starting out, it takes years to gain respect and be looked at as a person that people would want to use. And I don't think my gender at this point would have had anything to do with it.

"Hopefully Saturday will open more doors. But when it comes to me as a female jockey, I don't think I'm viewed any differently within the industry."

Osborne also said she is treated as "one of the lads" in the weighing room, and has never experienced sexism and misogyny unlike other female jockeys, including Bryony Frost.

Jockey Robbie Dunne was banned from racing for 18 months, with three months suspended, for bullying fellow rider Frost in 2021, which was later cut to 10 months on appeal.

Having ridden 60 winners since the start of May, Osborne is currently sitting eighth in the Flat Jockeys Championship, and is open about dreaming of being champion jockey in the future.

She would be the first female jockey to achieve that.

"You wouldn't be a jockey if you didn't want to be champion jockey one day. I think this is the first year that maybe I truly believe that I could one day," she said.

"It's been a phenomenal year that's been topped off by Saturday. But I'm very lucky. I have a very good agent [Tony Hind] and agents are so important in this sport. He's got an amazing book of jockeys, the likes of Ryan Moore, William Buick, Billy Loughnane. And I'm very lucky to be on his team.

"He makes champion jockeys, he's had a lot of them. And yeah, I would love to be the next one on the list."

Osborne makes history as first female jockey to win a Classic with St Leger victory

title: Why dealing with defeat is key for Lampard at Coventry
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains why Coventry boss Frank Lampard needs to manage himself as well as his players after their poor start to the season.
fullText:
Managing a newly promoted team in the Premier League is very demanding, as Frank Lampard is finding out at Coventry.

It's the highest level, not just for the technical ability of the players that your team faces but also the sheer physicality that these players possess, and it feels like the gap to the Championship is getting greater every season.

From my experience in the same situation, you have to be really smart in the way you approach each game and recognise the importance of preparation for each specific opponent, because your team has to be organised in possession, and definitely out of possession.

Teams in the Premier League counter-attack with greater efficiency so being solid behind your own attacking play is absolutely vital.

But the real advice I would give to managers in Frank's shoes is to manage yourself, and your own time, as well as your players.

I can tell you now that, whoever you are playing, if you get beaten - and especially beaten heavily like Coventry were by Brighton on Sunday - then it resonates with you. It's the same for every manager.

For Frank, whether it is losing at home to Hull or Brighton, or against Arsenal and Manchester City, then it will hurt.

But it is how he deals with those defeats that will decide what happens next.

Being the leader of a group of young men, you cannot look washed out and empty on a Monday morning after a heavy loss.

Yes, inside you will be hurting and your pride will be taking a bashing but everyone at the club will be waiting for your reaction, and will act accordingly.

Walking into the training ground in a dark mood and with your head around your backside just does not work, irrespective of what you are feeling inside.

I've been in that situation many times myself as a manager and what you have to do is puff your chest out and find a way of getting everyone back on track and working even harder with a set focus on the next game.

That's what all good leaders do. It is draining at times, but that is why managing your time and prioritising the issues that you can resolve is so important.

When I took Stoke up to the Premier League in 2008, I was learning on my feet.

We did not make a great start and I had to roll my sleeves up and get on with what I'd got in my squad, and really focus on getting results.

But away from that I was always forward thinking and I was quick at recognising what was needed to improve our chances of staying up.

When the window opened again in January, we were already in discussions with Tottenham for Matty Etherington, to supply us with crosses and chances from the wing.

We needed more goals too, so I took James Beattie from Sheffield United. They were a Championship side but that didn't matter because he had a record of scoring goals in the top flight.

We have heard so much about recruiting the right players in the right positions, and it is true today as it was in my day. Both lads played a significant role in keeping us up.

Coventry haven't scored a goal yet, and people might look in from the outside and feel the forward areas are an issue for them because the usual thinking is that the centre-forward has to lead the scoring charts, or a wide player or the number 10.

But the emphasis is on everyone to chip in and I would also reinforce one of the points I made in this column last season, about the importance of defending properly too.

On average, clean sheets earn you more points than scoring a goal, which is something I always stressed to my players. Nailing down the importance of both ends of the pitch is the narrative, whatever kind of run of results you are on, because games are won and lost there.

Coventry have made a poor start but what has happened in their first four games does not have to become the story of their whole season.

With Stoke, we got a win in our first home game - against Aston Villa - but that was our only victory in our first seven league matches after getting promoted.

The thing I remember most from that time is that Hull had come up with us and, after seven games, they had won at Newcastle, Arsenal and Tottenham and were in the top five in the table, while we were third or fourth from bottom.

I went out for dinner with my chairman, Peter Coates, and he said how Hull had made a wonderful start. I replied by telling him I bet you now that we finish above Hull... and we did.

The reason I thought that was because of the mindset of the team, and the fans.

I was confident my players were not going to go weak at the knees, and the togetherness we needed was already there in the squad, while the support was just off the scales, which helped us enormously at home.

Every defeat was taken on the chin, and accepted, but the lads were always ready to go, again and again.

It was Steve Coppell who said to me how you have to deal with the fact you are going to lose a lot of games - or at least not win a lot of them - when you take a team up into the Premier League.

It is a very unusual situation, to go from being in the Championship and winning regularly week after week, to dealing with defeat after defeat.

Steve told me to get ready for going on runs where we would not win for five or six games on the bounce, but then if we could win two or three games in the same period after that, we would fly up the table.

But getting your head around that is hard, and it is the same for the players who were part of that promotion - especially if you were dominant like Coventry were last season.

They were expected to challenge at the top of the Championship, but in my opinion over-achieved by finishing clear at the top.

It was different for Hull, who achieved a promotion under Sergej Jakirovic that no-one outside that club believed was possible.

They have started the season on fire, just like the Tigers did in 2008 when Phil Brown was in charge, and now they have to try to sustain it.

They are third at the moment but if they are 17th come the end of May, which is where they finished under Brownie, then that will be a successful season.

I will be taking a closer look at Hull's progress in this column in the weeks to come, as well as the other promoted team, Ipswich.

Gary O'Neil has a really tough gig at Portman Road but it is one he will relish. I gave Gary his senior debut with Portsmouth in the Championship in 1999 and he's a smart lad who was always football mad.

Ipswich are a great club and I hope both are successful this season. Gary has experience of the Premier League with Bournemouth and Wolves, and he is going to need it.

Including O'Neil, there are nine new managers starting with clubs in the Premier League. It's a bigger number than usual and I wanted to quickly run through all of them.

Enzo Maresca at Manchester City seemed like common sense to me, even before they started the season with four league wins out of four, because he has worked with Pep and the club before.

City had a large turnover of players with their ins and outs over the summer, but I'd expect them to be in the mix for all the trophies again this season.

Another place where lots of changes have taken place is Stamford Bridge. Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has experience of playing in England and will understand that no game in the Premier League is a shoe-in - as Saturday's draw with Hull showed us again.

Andoni Iraola did an amazing job at Bournemouth but he will need all of his managerial ability and acumen to succeed at Liverpool.

At Liverpool, teams will drop deep and rely on counter-attacking situations. At Bournemouth that did not happen very often.

So, Andoni has to prepare his coaching philosophy to overcome teams who will definitely play deeper and be much more defensive-minded against Liverpool than they were against Bournemouth.

In my opinion, given time he will a great success but as he prepares to take his new team back to face his old one at Vitality Stadium on Sunday, we are already seeing that Liverpool will need more changes to develop into the title-winning side that their fantastic supporters demand.

At Nottingham Forest, Oliver Glasner did a wonderful job at Palace and I am sure we will see more of the same at the City Ground.

At the moment I know less about Marco Rose, Matthias Jaissle, and Pierre Sage, at Bournemouth, Newcastle and Crystal Palace.

Unlike the other managers I have mentioned, they have no experience of the Premier League but they are all joining established top-flight sides which is a huge help.

Finally, there is Alvaro Arbeloa at Fulham. He had a fantastic playing record at Real Madrid and Liverpool and coached in the Real Madrid academy and their B team before taking charge of the first team for the second half of last season.

While he has not had much experience in the dugout, he has worked with many top managers and players.

Fulham will be a real test for him, as we've seen from the way they have started the season, so again they are a club I will be keeping a close eye on - but there are plenty of those!

I got stuck into lots of topics in this column last season, at all levels of the game and covering every aspect of management, but I'd love to know what you would like me to talk about over the next few weeks.

Please make any suggestions in the comments section below - and also feel free to ask me any questions too.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

title: A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel
description: Can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
fullText:
It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Neither was without controversy.

Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

The war was undoubtedly another.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.

"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."

Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'

"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

title: River home to 500 crocodiles chosen as Olympic rowing venue
description: A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles is given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.
fullText:
A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles has been given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.

The course on the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton, Queensland, has passed an independent technical assessment into its suitability.

The assessment did not consider the crocodiles but instead looked at "how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the Games".

The report was commissioned by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA), which noted, external that the Fitzroy River Flatwater Facility "is already a training and competition venue for flatwater sports, supporting school state championships, local regattas, and national team training camps".

As a recognised rowing facility, contingency plans are in place at events for when crocodiles are spotted and Olympic officials have previously been assured of rower safety.

World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide, formerly International Canoe Federation, both endorsed the course.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic Rowing," World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland said., external

Paddle Worldwide President Thomas Konietzko said: "The quality and depth of the technical work undertaken has significantly improved our understanding of the field of play and provides confidence to us and our athletes that the course can deliver fair competition for Canoe Sprint athletes."

Brisbane 2032 President Andrew Liveris played down the issue of crocodiles last year.

"There are sharks in the ocean and we're still surfing... it's a can do, not a can't do - please change the mindset here," he said at the time.

Speaking on Thursday about the venue having now been given the go-ahead, he said: "The endorsement provides additional certainty as we move into the next phase of venue planning and Games delivery, ensuring all future design and operational work continues to focus solely on Rockhampton."

Saltwater crocodiles - known locally as Salties - live in both freshwater and saltwater and can grow to be in excess of six metres long.

title: USA midfielder sues doctors after on-pitch cardiac arrest
description: United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last year.
fullText:
United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last year.

Midfielder DeMelo, who has seven senior caps for the USA, has filed a lawsuit against University of Louisville Health (UofL Health) for negligence.

The 28-year-old, who plays for Racing Louisville, collapsed in the first half of a National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) match on 14 September 2025.

According to documents, external seen by BBC Sport, the case was filed on Tuesday morning with Jefferson Circuit Court in Kentucky, where her club is based - a year and a day after her on-field collapse.

DeMelo's filing claims UofL Health and two doctors, Dr Sarabjeet Suri and Dr Jennifer Daily, "failed to act as a reasonably prudent and competent medical practice, and such negligence was a substantial factor in causing DeMelo to suffer severe physical injuries, including, but not limited to, her cardiac arrest".

Dr Daily, according to her online UofL biography, external, is Racing Louisville's chief medical officer. The lawsuit states DeMelo was under the care of Dr Daily from January 2024 to July 2026.

It states that in March 2025, Dr Daily referred DeMelo to Dr Suri for "evaluation and treatment" after she had been complaining of chest pain, dizziness and shortness of air; Dr Suri obtained a history, performed a physical examination and ordered diagnostic tests.

Nearly six months later, DeMelo suffered the cardiac arrest.

"She was subsequently diagnosed and treated for ventricular tachycardia [an abnormal heart rhythm]," the suit states.

DeMelo, who has spent her entire professional career with Racing Louisville, has not played since her collapse.

In a post to her Instagram page, external on Tuesday, De Melo - who was picked in the USA squad for the 2023 Women's World Cup and started their first two games - marked the anniversary of the incident.

"A year ago today, while playing soccer, I collapsed due to an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia, that caused me to go into cardiac arrest," she wrote.

"I respect and appreciate the privacy everyone has met me with while going through everything I have this year. I'll never be able to fully put into words how emotionally hard this year has been. There has been a lot of uncertainty and emotions intertwined with it all."

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

fullText:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Wednesday that Canada become the bloc’s first “associate member,” provoking a fresh tariff threat from US President Donald Trump.

The move is aimed at shoring up their economies in the face of increasing trade tensions with the United States. But Trump said Wednesday the US could put “heavy tariffs” on the European Union if he considers any new agreement with Canada to be a “hostile act.”

“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility,” he told reporters.

Canada is currently locked in a trade war with the US, its largest trading partner, adding urgency to efforts to get closer to the the European Union.

Trump has also repeatedly called for Canada to become the 51st US state, an idea firmly rejected by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Carney was a guest at von der Leyen’s state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, where she remarked that “in this new world we must urgently reimagine our partnerships and build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies.”

“In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible,” she said.

Carney, meanwhile, is keen to foster a much closer relationship with the EU, saying Sunday that Canada was pursuing a “unique alliance with the European Union.” He made headlines with a speech at Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year stressing the need for “middle powers” to act in concert amid a “rupture in the world order.”

Despite the backdrop, von der Leyen stressed Wednesday that the decision to join forces with Canada was “not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength,” though the EU has also been on the receiving end of Trump’s tariffs on allies over the past year.

It is unclear what elements associate membership might entail — or whether all EU member countries are supportive of the plan. Here’s what we know.

Canada, a member of the British commonwealth, shares deep cultural and historical ties to Europe and resembles European models when it comes to its parliamentary democracy, universal health care and social welfare, among other things.

Canada even shares a small land border with Europe, through Denmark on Hans Island, a small landmass off northwestern Greenland. The French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon also sits about 20 kilometers (12 miles) off the coast of Newfoundland.

But while Canada would likely satisfy the political, economic and legal standards for joining the bloc, there is one obvious barrier: It is not geographically in Europe.

To get into the EU, a country must follow a strict, multi-stage process called accession, and its candidacy must be unanimously approved by all 27 member states.

There is a queue of countries waiting to get in, with nine currently recognized as candidates for EU membership.

Other European countries, such as Norway and Switzerland, are not formal EU members but partner with the bloc on trade and open borders.

“Associate membership does not exist,” said Tinatin Akhvlediani, head of EU enlargement at the Center for European Policy Studies, a Brussels-based think tank. Countries including Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia have “association agreements” in place with the EU, but these entail alignment with the bloc’s laws, something Canada is unlikely to want, she told CNN.

According to a Wall Street Journal report at the weekend, among the things European and Canadian officials have discussed: reducing trade barriers; laying underwater cables linking Europe and Canada; redirecting pipelines to grant Europe access to Canadian gas; building new AI and tech infrastructure; and even granting Canadians the right to live and work in Europe visa-free.

Under these terms, Canada would have a relationship with the EU that is unprecedented for a country outside Europe. The EU’s ambassador to Canada told the Canadian Press last week that the partnership would be unlike anything that currently exists, without giving specifics.

In her speech, von der Leyen highlighted plans to cooperate on intelligent manufacturing, technology, defense, cyber security and artificial intelligence. Canada and the European Union would also work on energy, critical minerals and batteries, she noted.

The allies already share a substantial trading relationship, which has grown steadily since large parts of the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement came into force in 2017. However, the deal still needs to be ratified by 10 EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland.

Bilateral trade in goods and services reached €130.8 billion ($151 billion) last year, according to the European Commission, up more than 80% over the past decade. Major EU exports to Canada include cars, machinery and pharmaceuticals. Canadian exports to Europe include crude oil, fertilizer, critical minerals and base metals.

Carney, a former governor of the Bank of England, has strong ties in Europe from his banking days and has cultivated his relationships with like-minded European leaders since becoming prime minister in March 2025.

In Paris last year, during his first official foreign trip as leader — which was notably not to the US in a break from modern tradition — Carney described Canada as “the most European of non-European countries.”

Since then, several European Union countries have floated the idea of Canada joining the bloc, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who once called the possibility “a marriage made in heaven.”

Stubb and Carney reportedly text each other daily and are known for squeezing in a jog or a game of ice hockey between meetings on official trips.

“Wouldn’t it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?” asked Stubb, according to the Journal.

In March, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot raised the idea of Ottawa joining the EU, telling a conference that “maybe Canada at some point” will sign up, according to the Canadian Press.

That’s not to say all EU leaders would support Canada’s bid, and approval would require a unanimity that the bloc has often struggled to achieve.

The German government has already questioned whether the term “associate member” is even appropriate, although a spokesperson said it was open to discussing new partnership models with Canada, Reuters reported.

Carney received a standing ovation from lawmakers when he attended von der Leyen’s speech and is due to address European lawmakers Thursday.

Canadians are largely in favor of strengthening relations with the EU, though support for full membership remains split, according to recent data.

A survey conducted earlier this month by Canadian polling firm Abacus Data found about 80% of Canadians said Canada should deepen cooperation with the EU on foreign policy, defense and economic priorities — a six-point increase from when the question was last asked in February.

A further 56% of those surveyed said Canada has 

However, some in Canada are skeptical of cozying up to the EU, fearing it could further isolate Canada from its southern neighbor and largest trading partner, while others are concerned about a loss of sovereignty.

Pierre Poilievre, the leader of Canada’s opposition Conservative Party, called Carney’s effort to deepen ties with the EU “out of touch.”

“We will NEVER be the 51st U.S. state. And we will NEVER be the 28th EU state,” he wrote this week in a post on X.

title: Flash flooding kills 3 people in New Mexico as Southwest faces more dangerous rain
description:
Flooding is seen in the Crownpoint District of New Mexico in an image posted by the Navajo Police Department on Tuesday. - From Navajo Police Department
The Southwest faces a barrage of intense rain this week as rounds of storms are tapping into unusually moisture-rich air being pulled north from Baja California, after flash flooding in New Mexico killed three people early Wednesday.
Officers responded at around 12:30 a.m. local time to a report of three people washed away by flooding near Newcomb, New Mexico, on the Navajo Nation.
fullText:
The Southwest faces a barrage of intense rain this week as rounds of storms are tapping into unusually moisture-rich air being pulled north from Baja California, after flash flooding in New Mexico killed three people early Wednesday.

Officers responded at around 12:30 a.m. local time to a report of three people washed away by flooding near Newcomb, New Mexico, on the Navajo Nation. Police discovered two adults and one juvenile on scene, the Navajo Police Department said in a statement. All three were pronounced dead. The department declined to provide further details about the deaths when contacted by CNN, citing concern for the family’s privacy.

🌧️ Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app

Rainfall over Newcomb began Tuesday afternoon around 4:30 p.m. and lingered intermittently until just after midnight. The area saw around 0.5 inches to 1 inch of rain in total, with most of it falling within an hour Tuesday evening.

Wednesday’s storms prompted a rare Level 3 of 4 risk of flooding rainfall for parts of Arizona and New Mexico, including Phoenix and Tucson. Phoenix had not faced a flood risk that high since 2022.

More than 3 inches of rain fell in just three hours around the Phoenix metro area midday Wednesday, flooding multiple locations in the Phoenix area.

Officials reported inundated roads and stranded vehicles where drivers had to be rescued in Scottsdale and Mesa, CNN affiliate KPNX reported. First responders were called to a water rescue just south of Phoenix for a car stuck in floodwater with two people inside, CNN affiliate KTVK reported, citing the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office.

Rain chances will drop sharply around Phoenix Thursday as drier air moves in. Farther southeast, storms could still produce locally heavy rain, particularly south and east of Tucson.

Western and central New Mexico will remain vulnerable to flash flooding Thursday as more storms develop in the afternoon and evening, especially over the mountains. Repeated downpours over the same areas could send water rushing through normally dry arroyos and low-water crossings.

The heavy rain threat will gradually diminish in New Mexico Friday and Saturday as drier air spreads east.

️⛈️☔️In one of the impacted areas? Track the storms, find out your local risk and get more detailed timing from meteorologists in the CNN Weather app⛈️☔️

Soil across the region is generally dry and compacted, so rainfall quickly runs off the surface rather than soaking in. When combined with steep and narrow terrain, that runoff can quickly turn into fast-moving flash floods, sometimes far from where the heaviest rain actually fell.

New Mexico’s Sacramento Mountains near Ruidoso are particularly at risk for flash flooding and debris flows due to the wildfire-scarred ground that absorbs even less water than the surrounding terrain typically does. The fast-moving mix of mud, rock and burned vegetation can be even more destructive than floodwater alone.

Hikers at the Grand Canyon, Utah’s Zion National Park and other wilderness areas s hould be on alert for sudden flooding, since normally dry ground, including slot canyons, can quickly fill with surging floodwater.

This flooding is unfolding during the Southwest monsoon, when shifting winds pull moisture into the US Southwest, fueling thunderstorms. The monsoon season typically runs from mid-June through September, with the region now in its final stretch.

But this bout of torrential rain is being enhanced by a tropical disturbance that tracked up the Gulf of California and is now in northern Mexico. The system is providing extra moisture and energy for storms to tap into.

Extreme rainfall is becoming more common as planet-warming pollution pushes global temperatures higher because warmer air can hold more moisture.

This story has been updated with additional information.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down," the president told reporters on the tarmac in North Carolina.

fullText:
A federal judge blocked Trump's name from being added to the building.

President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the Kennedy Center could "close" or be "ripped down" if his administration doesn't receive recognition on the performing arts center as tensions over his name being removed mount.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down," the president told reporters on the tarmac in North Carolina.

Trump claimed that the Kennedy Center was a "mess" without his intervention and "has lost 10s of millions of dollars, even hundreds of millions of dollars," comparing it to New York's Carnegie Hall.

The president's comments come after a federal judge on Tuesday blocked the performing arts center's board from adding a tribute to Trump on the building or site. He responded by saying he wouldn't spend congressionally approved funding for the center's renovation unless the building also bears his name.

Congress last year appropriated $257 million for the renovation.

About an hour after the judge's ruling Tuesday, the board, which is controlled by Trump appointees, voted to close the center immediately for renovations, citing safety concerns after a piece of plaster from the ceiling of the grand foyer fell during a heavy rainstorm earlier this month.

On Tuesday, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, said Trump “threw a tantrum because he lost in court” when discussing the Kennedy Center meeting.

“He wasn't pleased with it. He was very explicit with his words, and I responded equally as explicit. He is in contempt of court for what he's doing now in trying to just simply go over and close the Kennedy Center and to have people leave the center,” Beatty told reporters on the House steps Tuesday night.

Beatty said “there was a heated debate” during the meeting.

On Wednesday, fencing was seen being installed around the main building's entrance.

title: What can the Nets expect to see from Mikel Brown Jr. this NBA season?
description: Brooklyn Nets rookie guard Mikel Brown Jr. seems to have some hype surrounding him so what can be expected from him this upcoming NBA season?
fullText:
Brooklyn Nets rookie guard Mikel Brown Jr. is coming into his first NBA season with a significant amount of hype after his promising freshman season at the University of Louisville. Brooklyn selected Brown with the No. 6 overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft after he proved that his back issues were behind him so what can be expected from the young guard?

"Brown, a 6-foot-5, 190-pound point guard from Louisville, will be bringing more than his physical skills to the Nets' young core," Steve Aschburner wrote on Brown for NBA.com. With training camp less than two weeks away, Brown has the chance to compete for the starting point guard spot along with players like Nolan Traore and Ben Saraf, two players from Brooklyn's 2025 draft class.

"He got some master-class tutoring from former NBA All-Star Rajon Rondo, a Louisville native. 'I was fortunate enough to have him as a mentor,' Brown Jr. said," Aschburner continued. "'He invited me to his crib, and we watched some film together, played a little bit of chess. … I got to pick his brain a lot.' Top lesson? 'Make the simple play.' Brooklyn needs that from Brown to improve on its total of 20 victories last season."

Brown, 20, is coming off a freshman season with the Cardinals where he averaged 18.2 points, 3.3 rebounds, and 4.7 assists, and 1.2 steals per game while shooting 41.0% from the field and 34.4% from behind the three-point line. After being drafted, Brown went on to show why the Nets chose him as he put up 15.0 points, 1.5 rebounds, 4.0 assists, and 1.2 steals per game while shooting 38.8% from the floor and 34.6% from deep in Brooklyn's summer circuit.

With forwards Michael Porter Jr. and Julius Randle in the fold, someone like Brown will be tasked with running the offense while he grows as a scorer to pair with his passing. It remains to be seen if Brown is able to earn the starting point guard job under head coach Jordi Fernandez, but even if he doesn't, the rookie should get plenty of runway to show what he can do at the NBA level.

title: Jets suspend Connor Hellebuyck for 'failure to report to training camp' after trade request
description: It appears the Connor Hellebuyck situation has escalated in Winnipeg.
fullText:
It appears the Connor Hellebuyck situation has escalated in Winnipeg.

The Winnipeg Jets announced Wednesday they have suspended the three-time Vezina Trophy-winning goaltender for a "failure to report to training camp." Their general manager Kevin Cheveldayoff will also speak with reporters Thursday morning to address the matter.

Hellebuyck went public with a trade request in August, releasing a statement confirming he had privately requested a trade months earlier and said a move out of Winnipeg is "the best path forward for me and my family."

In response, the Jets released a statement from Cheveldayoff saying the organization will "continue to work through the situation in a thoughtful manner."

Per TSN, the Buffalo Sabres held trade talks with the Jets ahead of the 2026 NHL Draft in June, with no discussions since. The Jets reportedly believe they have not received any offers with "fair value in return for an elite-level goaltender in Hellebuyck with years remaining on his contract."

Hellebuyck is currently playing on a contract that pays him an average of $8.5 million through the 2030-31 season. He had a down season last year, but has overall been one of the best goalies of the current decade, with Vezina wins in 2020, 2024 and 2025 and a Hart Trophy in 2025. He is set to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom as well, for his heroics in Team USA's gold medal run at the 2026 Olympics.

While they have not yet granted Hellebuyck's request, the Jets appear to be preparing for a life without him. They signed former Pittsburgh Penguins goalie Stuart Skinner to a two-year, $7.5 million contract over the summer, giving them either a potential starter or a backup to either Hellebuyck if he changes his mind or a starter they acquire in a hypothetical trade.

The Jets are set to officially begin training camp on Thursday.

"I'm not really championship-chasing, trying to find the best team I could win. I didn't want to put on a thousand jerseys," Leonard said.

title: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough
description: Researchers at Stanford University genetically altered mice to be able to receive and function with human brain cells.
fullText:
Neuroscientists in the US have successfully adapted mice to have functioning human cells inside their own brains.

The researchers hope that potential treatments for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental diseases that only occur in humans could now be tested on the laboratory rodents.

While mice with brains that are partly human might sound like a Kafkaesque experiment, the scientists said these are not "mice that think like humans".

The animals are genetically engineered - and surgically altered - so that some of their brain tissue is human.

The scientists said their work, published in the journal Nature, was carried out with independent ethical scrutiny.

The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective treatments.

Some conditions cannot be studied in a mouse, simply because rodents do not develop some of the brain disorders that we do.

As lead researcher Prof Sergiu Pașca from Stanford University explained in a press conference, psychiatry has "one of the lowest success rates for clinical trials".

"Even drugs that actually make it to clinical trial - that seem to be working really well in animal models - fail dramatically in clinic," he said in a press conference. "That tells us we're missing a lot of information about human biology and capturing that will be essential."

The Stanford researchers said that, for some complex conditions, including epilepsy, autism and cerebral palsy, it has the potential to be "transformative".

Pașca said: "Here we have a new model that allows us to actually capture aspects of human brain function in a way that has not been possible before."

The human brain is made up of billions of cells, interconnected in millions of circuits, making it difficult to understand its development and what exactly is happening – at the cellular level - when things go wrong.

While this research is not the first time human neurons have been implanted in laboratory rodents, these scientists took that approach to a new level.

First, they genetically-engineered mice to develop almost none of their own cerebral cortex – that is the outer layer of the brain sometimes referred to as "grey matter". It handles higher-level thinking, memory and senses.

The researchers then used skin cells taken from humans and "reprogrammed" them, so they grew into pieces of brain-like tissue.

These are structures called organoids – they are not whole brains grown in dishes, more collections of connected, living cells.

When these organoids were implanted into the mouse brain the cells divided and organised themselves into the animal's existing brain circuitry, connecting with the rest of the mouse's brain and spinal cord.

The cortex of the implanted mice is not perfect - normal cortex forms organised, structured layers. And as neuroscientist Dr Ilary Allodi put it, scans of these human-mouse brains look "a bit messy".

After a few months though, the human cells started to look and function like the outer layer of the mouse's brain.

About six months after the surgery, scientists put the mice through some basic behavioural tests - observing them as they moved around a small table-top arena.

Pașca said they performed "largely as [the normal] mice did".

"They don't have any enhancement," he added.

Dr Sarah Chan, a reader in bioethics at the University of Edinburgh who was not involved in this research, told BBC News there was "no indication that what's being created here are mice that can think like humans, or a human brain in a mouse body."

But she said the study "prompts us to think about what it might mean when we start changing animal cognition".

"How can we know what it's like to be one of these mice? And how do we take account of that in the ways that we treat laboratory animals," she added.

Dr Ilary Allodi, a neuroscientist from St Andrews University, who was not involved in the research, said the work the scientists had done was "very impressive".

In particular, Allodi pointed to the fact that cell types that are found only in human and other primate brains - not in the brains of mice – spontaneously formed in the implanted mice.

"You're keeping the human program inside the mouse environment – like the mouse is an incubator," she told BBC News.

These mice, which the researchers said are engineered and reared under strict ethical and welfare guidelines, will most likely be used in a small number of labs for studies of a few, very specific brain disorders.

Prof James Ainge, a neuroscientist who is also at St Andrews University, pointed out that while the development was technically very impressive, these mice could be "of limited use".

This, he said, was partly due to the "ethical issues of raising living human brain tissue in a mouse and what that would mean for the experience of the animal".

Neuroscientists who study the human brain, Allodi pointed out, all struggle with the same limitations. "We try to understand human disease, and what we have is mice, cells that live on a plate, and neural networks on a computer.

title: Xcode-Project-Format
description: A Swift library for reading, writing, and manipulating Xcode's JSON-based project.xcproj format.  - apple/xcode-project-format
fullText:
xcode-project-format is a Swift library for reading, writing, and manipulating Xcode's JSON-based project.xcproj format. It models the format as a rich set of value types nested under a single namespace, XCSchema, so consumers get precise, typed access to a project's structure instead of hand-parsing JSON.

The goal is to give the ecosystem a shared, accurate model of the Xcode project format — so tools like generators, linters, verifiers, and validators don't each have to reverse-engineer the format from scratch.

The package also ships xcprojformatter, a small CLI tool built on the library.

Add the package as a dependency in your Package.swift:

You'll find types for folders, file references, groups, targets, build phases, build rules, and the rest of the Xcode project model within this package.

The project documentation is available at Swift Package Index.

We welcome contributions within a defined scope. See CONTRIBUTING.md for what we accept, what's out of scope for now, and how to get started.
