title: Ctenophores: Wonders of Biology
description: Comb jellies are helping answer fundamental questions in biology, from how the earliest nervous systems evolved to how bioluminescence works.
fullText:
Around 700 million years ago, a group of organisms resembling little more than glowing, gelatinous blobs split off from the rest of the animals, forming possibly the earliest branching animal lineage. Nearly 200 species of ctenophores, commonly known as comb jellies (but unrelated to jellyfish), live today in environments ranging from the cold depths of the sea to warm coastal surface waters. Their magic isn’t just in their persistence or iridescence; it’s in their DNA.

Over the past decade, ctenophores have helped answer long-standing questions about fundamental biology, from how early nervous systems evolved to the origins of the mesmerizing phenomenon of bioluminescence.

Having access to closely related species across such variable environments “lets you ask questions about how certain things evolved,” such as adaptation to high pressure or light-sensing genes, said Steven Haddock, a marine biologist who studies ctenophores at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.

“That’s one of the reasons why we work with ctenophores,” said Pawel Burkhardt, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Bergen who studies the origins and evolution of neurons and nervous systems. “They’re very exciting to work with, and they’re also extremely beautiful organisms.”

For more than a century, scientists thought that sponges, or porifera, were the first to branch off — the sister group to all other animals. But over the past two decades, evidence has emerged that ctenophores were earlier. In 2023 — after years of a “ping-pong game” between labs debating which group came first, Burkhardt said — a landmark paper analyzing chromosome organization found that ctenophores, not sponges, are the sister group, though this is yet to be fully settled.

What makes this all the more surprising is that sponges lack muscles and neurons, while ctenophores have muscles and exhibit evidence of a simple nervous system. “If you think about the earliest branching animal lineage, you would expect less complexity,” Burkhardt said. “That changes a lot of the assumptions [about] how the very first animal may have looked.”

The more researchers investigate comb jellies, the more complex they appear and the more we learn about the origins of animal life. Some species have recently been observed reversing their development from adult to larval stages. Others have special types of lipids that help them withstand extreme pressure in the deep sea. They hold clues to the evolution of more and more complex body shapes.

It’s really important to study organisms that might seem strange or weird because they can tell us a lot about the physical, chemical, and biological principles of life, which can then be applied to ourselves, said Itay Budin, a biophysicist who studies cell membranes at the University of California, San Diego. “We are as distantly related to a ctenophore as a ctenophore is to a jellyfish.”

title: 'Resident Evil' review: Zach Cregger's video game adaptation is easily the best 'Resident Evil' movie yet
description: Austin Abrams in Zach Cregger's Resident Evil. (Sony Pictures Releasing /Courtesy Everett...
fullText:
There have already been seven Resident Evil movies — six of them in a more action-oriented series starring Milla Jovovich, four of which were directed by her husband, Paul W.S. Anderson, plus an unrelated "reboot" in 2021 called Welcome to Raccoon City that went for more of a John Carpenter vibe and was more of an attempt to truly "adapt" the games. There's also a Netflix TV show version that ran for a single season in 2022. Countless other works in the horror genre have unofficially cribbed from the Resident Evil games over the years. It's an incredibly influential series.

And yet, Zach Cregger, hot off his Oscar-winning original horror film Weapons, is the first filmmaker to truly feel like he's adapting the experience of playing the games, arguably the scariest survival-horror ones ever made, rather than simply incorporating story and plot elements to explain the outbreak of infected people. In Cregger's hands, Resident Evil is pure crowd-pleasing popcorn cinema, best experienced in a packed movie theater with dozens of other people reacting loudly to the madness.

The premise couldn't be simpler — and the runtime a brisk 90ish minutes — as we follow a medical courier named Bryan (Austin Abrams, proving himself to be the Bruce Campbell for a new generation) who unwittingly finds himself fighting for survival as one fateful, horrifying night collapses around him in a swirl of chaos. Fans of the video games will recognize various easter eggs and nods to game mechanics, including the importance of conserving ammo and checking every last drawer for more of it.

But you don't need to be familiar with the games at all to enjoy the movie, which is an efficient horror set-piece machine that just keeps putting Abrams in increasingly concerning situations. I can't stress enough how much this is a one-man show anchored by Abrams, and he crushes it. He's in every scene, earning tons of laughs simply by reacting as a normal person would in this situation; he's a true audience-surrogate character, ushering us through the chaos. His comedic timing, paired with Cregger's assured camerawork and editing, is a match made in genre-movie heaven.

I didn't expect it to be so heavily inspired by genre classics like The Thing and Evil Dead. In fact, it's a better Evil Dead movie than the last several movies with "Evil Dead" in the title, nailing the horror-comedy tone that only Sam Raimi and a few others can pull off with aplomb. Cregger has a ton of fun with the various monstrous forms that the infected take here, from fusing multiple humans together to crafting his own horror take on a big, scary guy like Dune's Baron Harkonnen. Resident Evil movies have thus far treated the zombies as pretty traditional movie zombies; Cregger's version gets at the attempt to create the next stage of human evolution.

Zach Cregger's Resident Evil may not feature characters that gaming fans recognize, but it's spiritually

description:
(Bloomberg) -- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union. 
Most Read from...
fullText:
(Bloomberg) -- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union.

US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms

MBS and Saudi Arabia Face Crisis With Key Oil Pipeline Shut for Weeks

Trump Jr.'s Wife Says Russian Paid for Parties But Not Wedding

Apple Just Launched Its New iPhones. Here Are 16 More Products Coming Soon

Crypto Stocks and Tokens Drop After Senate Blocks Landmark Bill

She offered the invitation during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance.

"In this new world, we must urgently re-imagine our partnerships and build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies," von der Leyen said. "I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the European Union."

Carney warned earlier this year that the "rules-based international order" was effectively dead and has made repeated calls for so-called middle powers to band together to oppose the pressure tactics and intimidation of the world's dominant economies. Bloomberg reported earlier that the transatlantic allies were in talks to forge a new alliance to ensure their security.

Von der Leyen also discussed closer cooperation with Canada on manufacturing, tech, defense and energy, and cited the Arctic as a "flagship joint project."

Canada's priority list includes concluding the ratification of CETA, the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, an accord that was negotiated a decade ago but that still hasn't been formally approved by 10 European countries, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Outstanding issues also include ironing out differences over EU's carbon pricing tool on imported goods, its deforestation and pesticides rules.

Canada, unlike the UK, has been granted access to SAFE, the bloc's €150 billion ($173 billion) loan program for defense procurement.

Canada and the EU will be expected to make progress ahead of their summit in Montreal in October, at which they could sign a digital trade agreement that it's been in the works, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"Europe and Canada believe in democracy," von der Leyen will say. "That power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest."

--With assistance from Max Ramsay.

title: U.S. military releases video of massive operation to rescue airman inside Iran
description:

The footage documents portions of the massive April operation to rescue the two-man crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle, call sign Dude 44, after the fighter was shot down by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile.
The pilot, known as Dude44 Alpha, and the backseat weapons systems officer, Dude44 Bravo, ejected from the aircraft and landed miles apart, leaving both stranded inside Iran.
fullText:
The U.S. military released dramatic new video on Tuesday showing parts of one of the largest combat search-and-rescue operations in its history, including the moment elite Air Force pararescue operators reached a badly injured American airman stranded deep inside Iran.

The footage documents portions of the massive April operation to rescue the two-man crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle, call sign Dude 44, after the fighter was shot down by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile.

The pilot, known as Dude44 Alpha, and the backseat weapons systems officer, Dude44 Bravo, ejected from the aircraft and landed miles apart, leaving both stranded inside Iran.

While Dude44 Alpha was rescued after a little more than six hours, Dude44 Bravo suffered a broken back, arm and shoulder after a damaged parachute led to a hard landing. He remained stranded for nearly two days before U.S. forces reached him.

HOLLYWOOD LEGEND MAKING MOVIE ABOUT EPIC IRAN RESCUE MISSION TO SAVE F-15 FIGHTER JET CREW

The newly released video shows U.S. military helicopters searching for Bravo as American forces worked to locate and recover him.

Despite his injuries, Bravo moved away from his landing site and began climbing toward a roughly 7,000-foot ridgeline as daylight revealed the desert valley and steep cliffs surrounding him.

The footage also shows American bombers and drones striking Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces that were in close proximity to Bravo.

TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS

"There was clear intent out of the Iranian ground force to come find those two guys," Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine told CBS News this week.

The video then shows the dramatic moment on April 5 when two elite Air Force pararescue operators, known as PJs, reached the injured Bravo on the mountain ridgeline.

Two large search-and-rescue aircraft had landed on a makeshift desert runway before smaller "Little Bird" helicopters flew toward Bravo's position on the ridgeline.

Bravo called the moment he saw his rescuers "one of the greatest moments of my life."

HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY

"Let's go," he recalled telling them.

The second rescue operation put 92 U.S. service members on the ground in Iran, marking the first time American forces had boots on the ground in the country since 1980.

Hundreds of U.S. service members also supported the operation from the air, while between 3,000 and 5,000 service members supported the rescue mission overall, according to U.S. Central Command Commander Adm. Brad Cooper.

But the operation was not over once Bravo was reached.

The landing gear of the two rescue aircraft became trapped in the desert sand, stranding Bravo and more than 90 U.S. service members inside Iran. A clandestine Air Force unit was ultimately brought in to extract the group, CBS News reported.

Bravo was finally brought to safety roughly 50 hours after Dude 44 was shot down. The rescue was completed as the sun rose on Easter Sunday.

Fox News' Liz Friden and Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

title: House speaker sends lawmakers home early ahead of midterm election recess
description: The speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, speaks to reporters at the US Capitol on 16 September 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty...
fullText:
The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess.

The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie's resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence.

It's the latest round of cancellations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday.

"I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis," the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch.

Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump.

"We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI," Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. "Because then we will lose our edge to China, and ​that has serious national security implications for every American family."

More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson, via a letter, to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards.

In a notice on Wednesday, House leadership told members that other votes on EPA regulations, originally planned for Thursday, would instead take place on Wednesday afternoon.

A spokesperson for Johnson characterized the House speaker's latest move as simply moving up scheduled votes, not canceling future votes.

Speaking to reporters outside of his office on Wednesday, Johnson said he was modifying the schedule because "the House has done its work". Johnson said he wanted members to return to their districts to spend time with constituents ahead of the election.

"You've seen the statistics we've been talking about for the last few days. This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789," Johnson said, repeating a claim he also made earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention.

However, so far, the current session has fallen short of passing legislation to surpass the two previous House sessions, according to the fact-checking website Snopes.

Johnson also addressed Massie's impeachment resolution, calling it "a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention". The House speaker insisted it would be "immediately" postponed and he would not address it before the recess because the US is in the middle of international conflicts.

Lawmakers will likely face a busy legislative agenda when they return to Capitol Hill after election day in November. Among their priorities will be addressing Massie's resolution on impeaching Hegseth because it was filed as privileged, which fast-tracks the resolution.

title: U.S. confirms it has weapons orbiting Earth for the first time
description:
Clipped From Video

“Today we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink told attendees of the Air, Space and Cyber Conference, an annual gathering hosted by the Air & Space Forces Association in National Harbor, Maryland. “This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”

fullText:
The United States has deployed weapons in space and will use them to defend American forces, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday. It’s the first public acknowledgment that the nation has such capabilities in orbit and a potential signal to those that could pose threats in the domain.

“Today we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink told attendees of the Air, Space and Cyber Conference, an annual gathering hosted by the Air & Space Forces Association in National Harbor, Maryland. “This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”

Meink did not provide specifics on the weapons and, when asked to expand, refused to provide additional details. It’s unknown when the weapons were put into orbit.

If the disclosure is meant to serve as a deterrent — aiming to warn adversaries that the US is capable of forcefully responding to threats in space — the vagueness of Meink’s remarks may limit their effectiveness, said Clayton Swope, the deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the bipartisan nonprofit Center for Strategic and International Studies, who previously served for more than a decade in the CIA.

“The disclosure is still significant because it’s not something that we have talked about in this way,” Swope said. But “you really have to think out this chain of logic beyond just this disclosure.”

For such a disclosure to be an effective deterrent, Swope said, US adversaries have to understand “what exactly is the destructive potential of this weapon, and then what exactly don’t we want them to do — so that by knowing that they don’t do it.”

President Donald Trump has touted the US Space Force, which he created in 2019 under the Department of the Air Force, as a historic step toward bolstering the nation’s defense capabilities amid an advancing arms race in which China and Russia have challenged America’s dominance in space.

“China develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy,” the US Space Force says on its website, while “Russia views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts.”

US military officials have repeatedly warned the two countries are testing new offensive space capabilities, citing examples such as Russian satellite constellation training missions that Washington says could demonstrate “attack and defend tactics” for future combat and China’s development of a nuclear capable partial-orbit hypersonic missile.

While the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons or weapons of mass destruction in orbit, it does not prohibit the use of conventional weapons in space or the use of ground-based weapons against assets in space — leaving room for interpretation.

It’s not clear what type of weapon the US may have deployed. There are a broad range of possibilities — including satellites capable of jamming enemy communications and weapons that could leave orbit, target and destroy ground-based equipment, Swope said.

It’s even possible Meink could have been referring to an anti-satellite weapon, or ASAT, which can be used to seek out and physically destroy an enemy satellite in orbit.

Such technology has been previously tested by the US, China and Russia. But it’s widely considered among the most risky and broadly detrimental types of space weapons because debris from exploded satellites can linger in orbit for years — risking setting off an indiscriminate string of collisions with any nearby satellites.

CNN has reached out to the Space Force for comment.

China called on the US on Tuesday “to stop expanding military build-up in outer space, and uphold global strategic stability with concrete actions.”

“China stands for peaceful use of outer space and keeping it safe, and opposes any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a warzone,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing on Tuesday.

The US committed in 2022 to never again test “direct-ascent” ASAT weaponry, Swope noted, referring to types of ASAT weapons that are launched from the ground to target a satellite.

But the precise language of the commitment does not rule out testing or deploying another type of ASAT weapon, such as a “co-orbital” ASAT weapon, Swope said. That type of tool could involve using a spacecraft to directly approach an enemy satellite in orbit.

“Dating back to the Soviet Union and the Cold War, the Russians have been interested in developing what I would call ‘co-orbital, anti-satellite’ weapons,” Swope added. “These are satellites that would launch some type of projectile or other munition at the target satellite to disable it.”

As CNN reported in 2024, US intelligence suggests Russia has also made efforts to develop a space-based nuclear weapon that would use a massive energy wave, known as an electromagnetic pulse, to potentially knock out a large swath of commercial and government satellites — a claim Moscow has denied.

Such a weapon could have broad, devastating impacts, such as upending satellites the world relies on to predict the weather and respond to disasters, or even potentially affecting global navigation systems used for a wide variety of purposes, including banking, cargo shipping, ambulance dispatch and even hailing a ride share.

“It is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space, and so we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that,” Meink said Monday.

Last December, Trump signed an executive order calling US superiority in space “a measure of national vision and willpower,” with an emphasis on developing next-generation missile defense technologies and ensuring its abilities to counter threats, including “any placement of nuclear weapons in space.”

The executive order was a step toward Trump’s proposed “Golden Dome” missile defense system, an ambitious multibillion-dollar plan inspired by Israel’s Iron Dome that officials say would allow the US to intercept missiles from anywhere in the world.

The US has remained vague on its plans for developing the missile shield, which Trump said he hopes will be completed by 2028. As CNN previously reported, the Pentagon has scheduled the shield’s first major test for just before the 2028 election, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Among other elements, the Golden Dome proposal includes deploying interceptors that could remain in Earth orbit until they’re used to destroy enemy missiles mid-flight.

Speaking Monday, Meink also said a US space-based interceptor program had moved “from initial contract to flight-ready hardware in less than one year,” without revealing further details.

CNN’s Rashard Rose, Simone McCarthy, Natasha Bertrand and Zachary Cohen contributed to this report.

title: 7 Republicans join Democrats in vote to rein in Trump's Iran war powers
description:

Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., introduced the war powers resolution that was backed by 14 of his fellow House Democrats, including Reps. Jason Crow, D-Colo, and Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash.
fullText:
A handful of House Republicans rebuked President Donald Trump's operation in Iran on Tuesday, joining Democrats to pass a resolution aimed at reining in the commander-in-chief's war powers.

Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., introduced the war powers resolution that was backed by 14 of his fellow House Democrats, including Reps. Jason Crow, D-Colo, and Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. But it was Republicans who helped put the legislation over the edge.

Seven House Republicans joined all 213 voting Democrats to pass the measure in a 220 to 204 vote late on Tuesday night. Opponents of the bill were 203 House Republicans and Rep. Kevin Kiley, I-Calif., who caucuses with the GOP.

"I've been consistent on that since the war powers provision expired after 60 days of engagement," Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital on Tuesday morning ahead of the vote.

REP TOM BARRETT: IT’S UP TO CONGRESS TO PREVENT ANOTHER ENDLESS AMERICAN WAR

Republicans who voted to withdraw U.S. forces from Iran have long argued that it's on Congress to declare war, not the White House. The War Powers Resolution of 1973 generally allows a president to engage U.S. forces in hostilities for up to 60 days without congressional authorization, with an additional 30-day withdrawal period under certain circumstances. Supporters of the resolution argue that period has already expired.

The Trump administration has argued the president is acting within his constitutional authority as commander in chief and has defended the continued military operation against Iran, saying the resolution would improperly restrict the president's ability to protect U.S. forces and national security interests.

The war in Iran has become a political lightning rod in the current midterm election season, dividing Republicans and providing political fodder for Democrats who have accused Trump of getting into another "forever war."

The conflict has also been blamed by some lawmakers and analysts for higher prices at the gas pump, which is expected to be a top issue for voters.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS OPPOSE THE IRAN WAR, SEE PROLONGED COMMITMENT

It also pushed Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a well-known critic of Trump's foreign entanglements, to try to force a vote on impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

But the vast majority of Republicans still stand by the president and insist he is well within his authority.

"The president has done a good job managing all this," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital. "We need to stand with the president right now and with the Iranian people. And the president's done what he promised the American people, that he wasn't going to let them have a nuclear weapon."

REPUBLICANS BREAK WITH TRUMP TO REBUKE IRAN WAR — BUT IT WON'T CHANGE POLICY

The Senate passed a similar resolution in June of this year, also with several Republicans defecting against Trump.

But even if an identical bill passes both chambers, Trump has indicated he opposes such legislation, meaning it would likely face a presidential veto if it gets to his desk.

In some ways, the surgeon general position – often referred to as the nation’s doctor – is the original health influencer, tasked with translating science into terms that are easy to understand and guiding the public on ways to improve their health.
fullText:
Wednesday’s Senate confirmation hearing wasn’t the first time much of the American public met Dr. Nicole Saphier and heard her perspective; President Donald Trump’s nominee for US surgeon general is a health and wellness influencer who has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers through her podcast and social media platforms.

In some ways, the surgeon general position – often referred to as the nation’s doctor – is the original health influencer, tasked with translating science into terms that are easy to understand and guiding the public on ways to improve their health.

“For a decade, I have specialized in translating complex, fast-evolving medical information on various media platforms into content that millions of Americans can understand and use, including during the uncertainty of the global pandemic,” Saphier, a radiologist and Fox News contributor, said in Wednesday’s hearing.

“I realized then how badly this country needs public health communication that is straightforward and grounded in the best evidence available,” she said. “My years of communicating directly with the public have prepared me to explain complex topics in a way that they can understand.”

But experts say that social media has changed how people receive health information, with increasingly blurred lines as to who is considered to have authority and expertise – and that bringing an influencer into the role of surgeon general presents both opportunities and challenges.

Dr. Jerome Adams, who served as surgeon general during Trump’s first term, says the distinction between the role of an influencer and the role of the surgeon general matters more than the overlap.

“An influencer builds a brand and an audience. The surgeon general speaks for the nation (and not just ‘followers’), leads the Public Health Service Commissioned Corps, and has a duty to follow evidence even when it is politically inconvenient,” Adams said in an email to CNN. “Influence is a tool, but it is not the job.”

The Pew Research Center said in a report published this year that a significant share of the American public – 4 in 10 adults overall and half of those under 50 – now get their health and wellness information from social media influencers and podcasts.

But the center’s analysis of thousands of influencer profiles found a wide range of backgrounds, with less than half describing themselves as some kind of health professional. About 1 in 8 cite their personal experience in their social media bios, and nearly 1 in 6 do not mention anything about their background or expertise.

“Now, when a healthcare provider sees a patient, any number of other individuals and platforms and messengers have that patient’s ears and eyes,” said Eileen Yam, director of science and society research at Pew. “The ballgame is changing so quickly as far as where people hear health information, wellness information, beyond that kind of mainstream white coat expertise.”

Influencers presenting information from a clinical perspective may take a very different approach from those who base their content around personal experience, experts say, and there may be friction between the two approaches on the same topic.

“On the internet, there’s a lot of anecdotal information that gets generalized, but not everything is generalizable,” said Amanda Yarnell, senior director of the Center for Health Communication at Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

“I think some of the most successful creators, both in audience and in providing good information and making people connect with it, are people who have blended their personal experience with other expertise,” said Yarnell, whose center launched a program in 2023 that works directly with creators to use their social media platforms to counter health misinformation online and to spread evidence-based science.

Surgeon general nominee Saphier presents herself as someone who can balance that line between personal and professional experience. To her nearly 360,000 followers on X, she identifies herself as a “full time wife, mom and doctor.”

Her Instagram profile, where she has 147,000 followers, includes the same line – but also indicates that she is the “creator of Drop Rx,” a brand of liquid herbal supplements.

Her bio page on the Drop Rx site says she wanted to create “clean, thoughtfully crafted tinctures that support focus, calm, balance, and overall wellness” that are inspired by “traditional herbal wisdom and modern scientific insight.” The site notes that “statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. Our products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.” Many of the products are currently unavailable online. Some sell for $24.99 for 2 fluid ounces.

Business interests like this are part of what has challenged influencer credibility, experts say, especially as more traditional information sources like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have also lost some of the public’s trust around evidence-based recommendations.

“There is often financial gain involved with (social media influencing), so that can influence the content that is delivered as well,” said Dr. Anne Cappola, ​a ​physician and executive director of the Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. “It’s not always transparent to those who are absorbing that information. It’s all getting muddy.”

Generally, Pew found that only about 10% of US adults say they trust all or most of the information they get from influencers, while a quarter said they trust not much or none at all.

“The lion’s share of these audiences say that they trust some of the information. So there’s some healthy skepticism that people are using when they’re seeing information from health and wellness influencers overall,” said Galen Stocking, an associate director of research at Pew and lead author of the recent report.

As the public parses all of the health and wellness information that is available to them online, experts say that trust in the messenger becomes one of most important aspects of who they decide to listen to.

“Authority, benevolence and integrity are three pillars of how people have long thought about trust models,” Yarnell said. “The way (these pillars) show up on the internet is quite specific, and they can be used for good or bad.”

Former Surgeon General Adams said the trust Saphier has gained as a health influencer could ​serve her well as surgeon general, but maintaining that trust in a government role under the current administration will present new challenges.

He said he isn’t concerned about Saphier’s ability to communicate, but he is concerned about whether “the environment she would enter will let her tell the truth about what’s actually harming Americans, and how best to protect them” – particularly around vaccine-preventable diseases.

Saphier will have to work harder to establish credibility with those who are skeptical about her “prior association with a network and movement that many see as increasingly against science and vaccines,” he said. But she has an opportunity to reach groups “who have tuned out traditional public health voices” and to “raise trust among people who currently distrust ‘the establishment.’”

She’ll need a “clear, independent voice,” he said.

When asked about her views on vaccines in Wednesday’s hearing, Saphier said that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is “our greatest tool for combating measles,” and she said she does not believe that childhood vaccines cause autism.

But when Sen. Bill Cassidy directly asked her “Should a parent be vaccinating their child with the MMR?” she didn’t reply with a yes or no.

“I think that the recommendation is to combat what we are seeing right now – the best tool we have to combat these infections, to save the most lives and to also create population herd immunity – is vaccination against the MMR,” Saphier replied.

In a podcast episode in February, Saphier reflected on the role of surgeon general after a prior nominee – author, Stanford medical graduate and wellness influencer Casey Means – faced her Senate confirmation hearing.

“The biggest skill that this person needs is they need to be able to effectively communicate with the public, public health messaging,” Saphier said on her podcast.

“But even more important than that, they need the respect of not only the people, the American people that they are communicating to, but they also need the respect of the administration for which they are working together with to get that research and put out the messaging, and also the medical professionals, the medical organizations, they need to make sure that she is a trusted messenger.”

Trump withdrew Means’ nomination in April after the vote stalled in the Senate, replacing her with Saphier. (Trump had previously withdrawn the nomination of another surgeon general candidate, Dr. Janette Nesheiwat, a New York family physician and former Fox News medical contributor.)

Within days of her nomination, Saphier deleted numerous social media posts in which she broke publicly with Trump and US Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on some of the administration’s most politically sensitive health issues, including vaccines and autism.

Saphier changed her X profile to private soon after.

“A preexisting following is useful only if she uses it to defend science, not to soften it,” Adams said. “Trust in this role has never come from celebrity. It comes from consistency with evidence, and a willingness to speak out on behalf of health, even when it may be unpopular.”

title: Obamas mourn death of 'cherished' family dog, Sunny
description:
President Barack Obama is mourning the loss of a "cherished" family member.
The former president, in a Wednesday, Sept. 16, post on Instagram, shared his pet dog, Sunny, who joined the family during Obama's second term in the White House and immediately won their hearts, has died. He did not share a cause of death.
Describing his pet of 13 years as a "force of nature," Obama joked the family "had trouble keeping up with her.
fullText:
President Barack Obama is mourning the loss of a "cherished" family member.

The former president, in a Wednesday, Sept. 16, post on Instagram, shared his pet dog, Sunny, who joined the family during Obama's second term in the White House and immediately won their hearts, has died. He did not share a cause of death.

Describing his pet of 13 years as a "force of nature," Obama joked the family "had trouble keeping up with her."

"Athletic and full of boundless energy, she leapt over the hedges on the South Lawn like they weren’t even there, chasing squirrels, birds and anything else that moved," Obama wrote. "And whereas the way to Bo’s (the Obamas' first dog) heart usually involved a treat, Sunny was more interested in having us run around with her, roll on the floor with her, or have her belly rubbed for as long as we were willing."

Obama said Sunny, a Portuguese water dog, loved his daughters, "even if they were pestering her when she was napping," and their team, who she would "often follow them around, helping them on the job."

"She was fiercely protective of Bo, who she rightly sensed wasn’t always as alert and attentive as she was," Obama said, adding that, other than Bo, she "preferred people to dogs."

Sunny also had her quirks. She was a loud and sloppy drinker, Obama said, and despite her breed, "she hated getting wet."

"But as far as our family was concerned, she was pretty much perfect, and for thirteen years, she would be by our side – always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure, still fiery and gorgeous till the very end of her days," Obama wrote. "We will miss her terribly, and imagine she’s with her big brother now, making sure he’s okay."

Born in Michigan in June 2012, Bo arrived at the White House in August 2013, USA TODAY previously reported.

The White House, at the time, had said Sunny was "the perfect little sister for Bo -- full of energy and very affectionate."

"The First Family picked her name because it fit her cheerful personality," it had said.

The family's first dog Bo, also a Portuguese water dog, died in May 2021 following a battle with cancer. He was a gift to the family from then-U.S. Sen. Ted Kennedy. The Portuguese water dog breed is hypoallergenic, according to the Portuguese Water Dog Club of America, which meshes well with the Obama family's allergies. Malia Obama, President Barack Obama's eldest daughter, suffered from canine allergies.

Obama, in a tribute at the time, said Bo had been "a constant, gentle presence in our lives—happy to see us on our good days, our bad days, and everyday in between" for more than a decade.

"He tolerated all the fuss that came with being in the White House, had a big bark but no bite, loved to jump in the pool in the summer, was unflappable with children, lived for scraps around the dinner table, and had great hair," he said. "He was exactly what we needed and more than we ever expected. We will miss him dearly."

Sasha and Malia named him after the first lady's father, who had a nickname of "Diddley," and their cousin's cat, whose name also was Bo. The White House had listed his hobbies as playing on the lawn and going on walks. His favorite food was tomato and, despite his breed, he couldn't swim.

This story was updated with more information.

Contributing: Sean Rossman, USA TODAY

Saman Shafiq is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach her at sshafiq@gannett.com and follow her on X and Instagram @saman_shafiq7.

title: The Kennedy Center is 'temporarily' closed — and a judge wants answers
description:
The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts is seen from the Georgetown Waterfront on September 15, in Washington, DC. - Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
One day after a dramatic meeting of the arts institution’s Board of Trustees, during which members – many of whom are allies of President Donald Trump – voted to close its doors, lights inside the Kennedy Center’s main building appeared to have been turned off.
The doors had been locked at 6 p.m.
fullText:
One day after a dramatic meeting of the arts institution’s Board of Trustees, during which members – many of whom are allies of President Donald Trump – voted to close its doors, lights inside the Kennedy Center’s main building appeared to have been turned off.

The doors had been locked at 6 p.m. Tuesday night and bike racks were stacked up by entrances to block public access.

But officially closing the public monument would violate a court order requiring it remain open as a lawsuit brought by Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty continues.

On Wednesday, US District Court Judge Christopher Cooper, in response to an appeal for an emergency hearing filed by Beatty, ordered the Trump administration to answer questions over the status of the building by Thursday at 10 a.m. ET.

Beatty issued the request after a member of her legal team was denied entry to the main building and “was informed by several security staff members that the building is currently closed to the public,” her attorneys said in a court filing.

A spokesperson for the Kennedy Center told CNN the building was “temporarily” closed due to safety concerns. But Beatty’s lawyers said that when they asked for an explanation from the Justice Department, they did not receive a reply – a violation of the court order, they contend.

When CNN visited on Wednesday, no signage was visible indicating any change of status to the main building – despite the fences and barricades over the doors.

A few security guards were outside as construction crews worked outside the building, where a fence with white curtains had been erected.

Outside the main building, the digital advertising boards still hype upcoming shows, and a landscaper was pruning the hedges. Employees came and went through a parking garage entrance. One of them told CNN that their badge worked for getting into the building – but only on the side doors.

A lone protestor stood outside with a sign that said: “There is still an injunction, remember?” And “shame on the Trump board.”

The relative calm of the scene at the center belies the drama that is expected to continue in the days to come.

The Justice Department has said it plans by Friday to appeal the court’s decision forcing it to remain open, while Trump has warned that the center may not reopen unless his name can be affixed to the building.

Trump later Wednesday seemed to raise the stakes if that effort fails: “It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape.”

Trump argued that his administration “should be recognized” for taking on the financial burden of fixing what he called “a mess.”

“For the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition,” he told reporters.

Meanwhile, an annex of the Kennedy Center, a separate arts space known as The Reach, remains open.

On Wednesday, the song “Jolene” was being played. A Dolly Parton celebration is planned for September 25.

When asked if it will remain open, a worker there replied, dryly: “We have no idea.”

This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Top Democrat places hold on Trump admin. plan to sell $2.8 billion in heavy bombs to Israel
description:
— The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Wednesday that he's going to block a proposed sale of $2.8 billion in heavy weaponry to Israel over concerns that the powerful bombs may not be used in line with U.S. and international law.
Rep.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Wednesday that he's going to block a proposed sale of $2.8 billion in heavy weaponry to Israel over concerns that the powerful bombs may not be used in line with U.S. and international law.

Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he would withhold approval for the sale because of "grave, unresolved concerns" about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government.

"The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with U.S. law and with appropriate protections for civilians," Meeks said in a statement. "I therefore will not clear this sale at this time."

Meeks' objections, however, will not likely affect the sale, which was informally notified to lawmakers on Tuesday. Once it is formally notified to Congress, Secretary of State Marco Rubio can bypass the normal congressional review process by making an emergency determination that the transaction is an urgent national security interest.

Rubio has done so in the past, including bypassing a normal congressional review process to approve a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel last year. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totaling $6.67 billion in January.

The State Department did not respond to requests for comment about either the new proposed sale or Meeks' objection to it.

The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 powerful 2,000-pound bombs, The Associated Press has reported. The transfer of 2,000-pound bombs had been paused by the Biden administration over concerns about the possibility of mass casualties.

The proposed sale is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israel's military capacity and it comes as Israel is facing increased international isolation over its war in Gaza in response to the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas.

The conflict in Gaza has left tens of thousands of Palestinians dead and has decimated the enclave. The U.S. brokered a fragile ceasefire, but violence has continued.

title: House panel votes to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt in Epstein probe
description:
The House of Representatives voted unanimously to hold hedge fund manager Leon Black in contempt of Congress after he did not appear for a deposition or turn over documents to lawmakers investigating the Jeffrey Epstein case.
The full House voted a day after the Republican-led House Oversight Committee took a similar vote unanimously and across party lines on Sept. 15. Epstein survivors applauded Chairman James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky, for his willingness to force the issue.
"No one is above the law," Comer said.
fullText:
The House of Representatives voted unanimously to hold hedge fund manager Leon Black in contempt of Congress after he did not appear for a deposition or turn over documents to lawmakers investigating the Jeffrey Epstein case.

The full House voted a day after the Republican-led House Oversight Committee took a similar vote unanimously and across party lines on Sept. 15. Epstein survivors applauded Chairman James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky, for his willingness to force the issue.

"No one is above the law," Comer said. "Mr. Black will be treated the same as anyone else in this investigation, and his actions have consequences."

Black founded the hedge fund Apollo Global Management but stepped down in 2021 after it became public that he paid Epstein $158 million for tax and estate planning. He was mentioned multiple times in the Epstein files released by the Department of Justice in February.

Comer said Black refused to comply with the committee's subpoenas to appear for a deposition, and a second one requiring him to turn over all nondisclosure agreements to which he was a party and ones that mention Epstein or Epstein's convicted accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell.

"Subpoenas are not suggestions," Comer said before the vote. "They carry the force of law and require full compliance. Mr. Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation because he maintained a close personal relationship with Epstein for years during the time when Epstein was engaged in sex trafficking."

Black has said in the past that he had a strictly professional relationship with Epstein. Additionally, Black's lawyer vehemently denied allegations against him after he was mentioned in the Epstein files.

USA TODAY reached out separately to Black's lawyer for comment.

A group of more than a dozen Epstein survivors including Annie Farmer and Dani Bensky issued a statement praising Comer for "showing real resolve" and "sending a clear message that wealth and influence do not put anyone beyond the reach of congressional oversight."

title: NBC L.A. helicopter's final broadcast could hold key clue to deadly crash
description:
On Wednesday, investigators examine the site of the NBC4 news helicopter crash in Chatsworth. (Kayla Bartkowski / Los Angeles Times)
It was a night of devastation in Chatsworth that began with a deadly Metro bus collision and ended with the fiery crash of an NBC4 helicopter covering the news that left two journalists and, on the ground, a bystander dead.
Tuesday’s scene was a mixture of confusion and chaos, with first responders fanned out across two catastrophes and television news teams desperately trying to find out whether their journalists were safe. The crashes  claimed the lives of five people and left others with various degrees of injury. 
Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration were trying Wednesday to determine exactly what caused the news helicopter, a Eurocopter AS350 B2, to go down.
fullText:
It was a night of devastation in Chatsworth that began with a deadly Metro bus collision and ended with the fiery crash of an NBC4 helicopter covering the news that left two journalists and, on the ground, a bystander dead.

Tuesday's scene was a mixture of confusion and chaos, with first responders fanned out across two catastrophes and television news teams desperately trying to find out whether their journalists were safe. The crashes claimed the lives of five people and left others with various degrees of injury.

Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration were trying Wednesday to determine exactly what caused the news helicopter, a Eurocopter AS350 B2, to go down.

NTSB Investigator Fabian Salazar said officials are searching through the wreckage, combing through maintenance logbooks, security footage, weather reports and witness interviews, and reviewing the pilot's training to figure out what went wrong.

But the most critical information so far has been audio captured from the helicopter during a live broadcast of reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw's final moments before it crashed.

The footage shows an aerial view of the bus crash with the whirl of the helicopter in the background. Suddenly, the sound of the engine's motor winds down and a horn blares, possibly warning the pilot that the main rotor speed had dropped too low or the helicopter had lost hydraulics. Moreno responds to the noise with a quiet "uh oh."

The angle of the camera begins to descend and Moreno is heard asking "You can't pull up?" before the video cuts out. Moreno, Marciniw and 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, who was on the ground when the chopper went down around 7 p.m., were killed.

"That video is probably the most important piece of evidence we have recovered so far," Salazar said.

Aviation experts told The Times the crash might be the result of a mechanical failure with the 22-year-old aircraft, a common helicopter for news and law enforcement organizations because of its general reliability.

Zoey Tur, a veteran news helicopter pilot who operated the type of helicopter the NBC4 crew was flying, said the sound the microphone picked up was of the engine shutting down.

"First, the engine starts winding down, which in turn reduces power to the rotor blades. Then you hear the horn warning of low rotor RPM. You can even hear the blade slap slow down," Tur said.

But, Tur pointed out, the fire that resulted when the copter crashed indicated there was still fuel onboard, so the engines likely shut down for another reason.

When a helicopter's rotors stop rotating, there's a safety maneuver known as autorotation where the pilot can try to gain enough momentum and upward flow on the rotor blades to increase their rotation, which helps control the aircraft as it descends, said Jack Cress, a former helicopter pilot for the U.S. Marine Corps and a helicopter accident investigation instructor at USC's Aviation Safety and Security Program.

Cress compared the maneuver to a fixed-wing airplane gliding through the air with the force generated by its wings but, in this case, the helicopter would use the upward force on its rotors caused by descending, or moving forward, to make the rotors turn fast enough to keep the craft in relative control.

But Cress said the fact that the helicopter appeared to be hovering in the air, and at a low altitude, would make it difficult for the pilot to execute the maneuver.

"In this case, he's in the worst part of the height-velocity curve," Cress said, referring to a chart used by helicopter pilots that tracks height and air speed for safe flight conditions. "That is a dangerous place to be."

Helicopter pilots are trained to stay away from those conditions, Cress said, because the lack of altitude and forward momentum give pilots little recourse if there is engine trouble. But for news helicopters and police choppers, hovering and maintaining low altitude is a common practice, he said.

Those conditions of hovering in the air, with little altitude and no momentum, are commonly referred to by helicopter pilots as a "dead man's curve," said Jeff Guzzetti, a former NTSB and FAA investigator who is also an instructor with USC's Aviation Safety and Security Program.

"That's the worst place to be if you have a problem," Guzzetti said.

The helicopter was owned by Tiny Bubbles Aviation Inc., a holding company with a business address listed at Whiteman Airport in Pacoima, according to state and FAA records. The company is listed as the owner of at least six aircraft, including five helicopters.

Lawrence Welk III, who is listed in public records as an agent of Tiny Bubbles Aviation, is also president of Welk Aviation, a company that according to its website owns and operates news helicopters for KNBC and KTLA.

In a brief phone call on Wednesday, Welk confirmed to The Times that the company was working with investigators but declined to comment on the incident.

"I just got back from the accident scene," Welk said.

Welk later issued a statement saying the Angel City Air Operation, which is listed as a division of Welk Aviation, was "devastated by the loss of two of our own and one bystander on the ground. ... Right now, our focus is on supporting our team and the families affected during this incredibly difficult time." Welk said the company was "cooperating fully" with the NTSB and FAA on their investigation and would not speculate on the cause of the crash. "We ask for privacy for the families and our team as we grieve together."

The bus crash brought an army of first responders and news media to the area, including TV news choppers flying overhead. Residents gathered around the bus to figure out what was going on.

Then, everyone heard an explosion and saw a fireball rising a few blocks away. Many ran to that scene, where a fire was raging. Firefighters tried to battle the blaze while police pushed back the public and reporters. There were rumors immediately that a news chopper had crashed.

NBC4 anchor Colleen Williams told viewers the station had lost contact with its chopper crew. Around 9 p.m., she confirmed the NBC4 team had crashed.

The helicopter went down between two commercial buildings in the 9100 block of Mason Avenue, smashing into a pair of truck cargo containers.

The situation thrust the team at NBC4 into a journalist's nightmare — a tragedy where reporters become part of the story.

"They were sacrificing their lives in service of their community," NBC morning anchor Lynette Romero told viewers, with her co-anchors by her side. "They were determined and dedicated until the very end doing the job they loved so much. Our hearts are heavy this morning but we are here with you, we are here for you as we try to navigate these tragedies together."

On Wednesday, authorities announced they had arrested Bailee Lynn Rios, who they said was driving the SUV that slammed into the bus, on suspicion of murder.

Rios, 36, is being held in lieu of $4 million bail, according to jail records.

Los Angeles police said Rios was driving a gray 2004 Ford Expedition around 5 p.m. Tuesday southbound in the northbound lanes on De Soto Avenue when she ran a red light at Nordhoff Street. The SUV narrowly avoided a car driving through the intersection before crashing into the side of the Metro Line 166 bus.

The violent crash ejected one passenger from the bus and partially ejected a second person, according to police. Two passengers, identified as 31-year-old Gage Weida and 46-year-old Daniel Castillo of Arleta, died at the scene.

One passenger, who suffered severe injuries, and five others with non-life-threatening injures were taken to hospitals.

The chain of events left residents shaken. "Anybody could be gone in a minute, you know?" Winnetka resident Michael Sanchez, a physical therapist, said.

The Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Wednesday, marking its first hike in more than three years, in a move that will likely make borrowing more expensive while giving savers a modest boost.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee announced a widely expected quarter-point rate increase and indicated another to come.

The stock market's reaction to the Fed's announcement is likely to draw the most headlines, and John Shugar, a partner at Goldman Sachs, leans toward an optimistic scenario.

"You basically have a market where all of the heavy lifting has actually been done on the earnings side," Shugar said in an analysis. He points to "terrific opportunities" in various AI consumer sectors, though "over the next few weeks, we may have a lot more speed bumps."

However, within one year, he says he expects the S&P 500 index to climb above 8,000.

What will a higher rate environment mean for your money? The federal funds rate influences not only the stock market, but also savings rates, interest charges, and, to a lesser degree, mortgage rates. Here's how to prepare for the impact on your deposits, credit, and debt.

A series of Fed rate hikes will likely lift deposit earnings, slowly. But deposit accounts are mostly for convenience, not substantial returns, and gains so far in 2026 have been meager.

Your checking account churns cash flow to pay bills. The liquidity limits your earning power.

The national average interest rate on checking accounts has barely budged this year, remaining at 0.07%. A Fed short-term interest rate increase, whenever it comes, may nudge earnings incrementally higher.

Interest rates on savings accounts are only marginally better, clinging to 0.38%. But savings accounts are for near-term money.

High-yield savings accounts have been more effective at paying interest. Rates are mostly in the 3% range, with an occasional 4% yield available.

This is one category where rate shopping and subsequent Fed rate increases really pay off.

Dig deeper: 10 best high-yield savings accounts

If you have $10,000 or more that you want to keep on the sidelines but easy to tap when you need it, money market accounts have been convenient — but low-paying, with a national average payout of only 0.63%.

A high-yield money market account is a better option, where you may still find a rate just under 4%, but mostly in the mid-3% range.

CD rates have begun inching higher. The national average on a 12-month CD is 1.71%, but you can find better deals if you're willing to shop around — and move your money to the best offer.

Your minimum deposit and term will affect your rate. Fed rate hikes may ultimately sweeten CD rates.

Learn more: The best CD rates on the market

And then there are mortgage rates, often the largest borrowing expense consumers face. Fed interest rate increases don't usually move mortgage rates directly — the bond market tends to price in hikes before monetary policy moves.

Mortgage rates hit three-year lows at the end of February and into early March. Then the war broke out in the Middle East, and rather than falling further, home loan rates reversed course and edged higher. Home loan rates have recently neared or topped 7% (depending on the rate reporting source), mirroring the higher yields of the 10-year Treasury note.

Housing industry analysts at the Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae predict that mortgage rates will remain above 6.5% through 2027.

Dig deeper: Mortgage rate predictions for the next 5 years

Personal loan interest rates have risen slightly to an average of 11.86%. Advertised personal loan rates are now generally in the 7%-8% range.

The Federal Reserve influences consumer loan rates by setting the federal funds rate, which affects how much banks charge each other for overnight lending. That cost typically gets passed on to borrowers through higher or lower rates on personal, auto, and student loans.

The Federal Reserve doesn't set student loan rates directly, but its federal funds rate influences the 10-year Treasury yield (which determines federal loan rates) and the prime rate (which determines private loan rates).

The federal funds rate doesn't directly determine federal student loan interest rates, but it can influence them indirectly. Congress sets the federal student loan rates based on the 10-year Treasury note, adding a fixed margin each year.

But the 10-year Treasury yield moves with investor demand, not the Fed's rate. When investors expect high inflation or strong economic growth, they demand higher yields, which can push federal student loan rates higher.

That said, if the Fed's rate hikes successfully cool inflation, Treasury yields may drop — and the following year's federal student loan rates could be lower.

Private student loans are offered by banks, credit unions, and online lenders, many of which use the prime rate as a basis for setting their interest rates. The prime rate moves alongside the Federal Reserve's rate decisions. So, when the Fed raises rates, new private loan rates usually rise, and when it cuts rates, they tend to fall.

Michele Raneri, vice president and head of U.S. research at TransUnion, expects consumers to see "minimally higher" borrowing costs as variable-rate credit products reflect the Fed's interest rate hike.

"A consumer carrying the average Q2 2026 credit card balance of $6,610 at a 22% APR could see an increase of $1.38 in minimum monthly payments as those higher rates are passed on," Raneri said in a statement. "While the near-term impact on minimum monthly credit card payments may be relatively small, higher borrowing costs can add up over time, particularly for consumers carrying larger balances or making only minimum payments.

Reducing revolving debt will limit the impact of rising interest rates, she added.

Yahoo Finance tip: The best way to earn a lower credit card interest rate right away is to ask. If you make regular payments and have seen your credit score improving, it's a good time to call your credit card provider and ask for a lower interest rate.

"There's an old Wall Street adage that says, 'Don't fight the Fed,'" Kevin Gordon, head of macro research and strategy at Schwab, said in an analysis. "The idea behind it was that there's often a lot of turbulence associated with Fed rate-hiking cycles."

He noted that history shows an average maximum loss of more than 10% for the S&P 500 sometime within 12 months after the start of a higher-interest-rate cycle.

"Broadly, though, we would say that the economic backdrop is still relatively favorable for the Fed to be hiking. So even if it is a hiking cycle where they do hike more than once, we think that the economy can probably hold up," he added.

Stock prices often react to the Fed's rate actions, but they are only one of many factors affecting the investing climate and stock prices. AI investments and oil-price-fueled inflation seem to be the most motivating factors for equity markets these days.

If you want to manage your investments for the current environment, monitor broader economic and corporate profit trends, as well as interest rates. If you prefer to stay conservative, fill your portfolio with high-quality stocks that have proven themselves in all economic cycles.

Then, wait patiently for long-term growth.

title: Trump slams Fed rate hike and says he told Warsh 'you might as well vote with the board'
description:
President Trump reacted to Wednesday's Fed rate hike, saying “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less" and acknowledging he discussed with Kevin Warsh the Fed chair's plans for how to vote ahead of time.
"I talked to Kevin and I said, ‘you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter,’" Trump told reporters Wednesday evening.
The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously Wednesday to raise rates by 25 basis points, its first hike in three years and the first under Warsh.
The president, who has spent more than a year calling for lower rates, first posted on Truth Social that rates should be dropping and that the trade deficit was a reason to "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" days after he threatened to stop trading with countries that have a trade deficit unless the Fed cuts rates.
fullText:
President Trump reacted to Wednesday's Fed rate hike, saying "Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less" and acknowledging he discussed with Kevin Warsh the Fed chair's plans for how to vote ahead of time.

"I talked to Kevin and I said, 'you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter,'" Trump told reporters Wednesday evening.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously Wednesday to raise rates by 25 basis points, its first hike in three years and the first under Warsh.

The president, who has spent more than a year calling for lower rates, first posted on Truth Social that rates should be dropping and that the trade deficit was a reason to "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" days after he threatened to stop trading with countries that have a trade deficit unless the Fed cuts rates.

Later Wednesday, when he was asked by reporters if he still has confidence in Warsh, Trump said he did, but said "he's got a very tough board." He called the FOMC "a bunch of politicians."

In a press conference Wednesday afternoon, Warsh demurred on the question of presidential involvement in the Fed decision, telling reporters, "I've got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

Trump's suggestion of his own role in the voting process came after the White House tried to telegraph a hands-off approach to the Federal Reserve in recent weeks, but saw Trump and his team quickly hit back at the decision repeatedly.

Senior Deputy press secretary Kush Desai also reacted to the move in an appearance on Fox News, calling it a "rather unfortunate decision by the Federal Reserve" that was "not backed by a particularly compelling economic case."

Trump has now repeatedly praised Warsh personally while also calling the FOMC "political" for not lowering rates. Just this past weekend, the president also again stated his view that the US should have the lowest interest rates in the world.

Warsh voted along with all of his colleagues on the committee to raise rates but didn't offer a projection about future rate hikes and dodged questions about politics and the president multiple times.

He called independence of the central bank a "two-way street."

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane…we'll let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too," he said.

The central bank also signaled that one more rate hike is likely before the end of the year, an acknowledgment that the Fed needed to step in to counteract price pressures.

title: Macklemore and Robert Kraft pledge millions amid Ed Sheeran tour controversy
description:
Macklemore on Wednesday pledged to donate the “entire $1 million” of his net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour to Palestinian relief organizations, days after he was dropped from the tour over his pro-Palestinian comments. 
He also invited New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who said Macklemore wouldn’t be welcome at Gillette Stadium for the tour's scheduled performances at the end of September, to match his donation. Within hours, Kraft released a statement saying Sheeran had already asked him to match his $2 million donation to humanitarian aid in the region. 
Their statements come amid a growing controversy following Macklemore’s removal that has seen all of Sheeran’s supporting acts quit the tour. Sheeran is set to play in Philadelphia this weekend.
fullText:
Macklemore on Wednesday pledged to donate the "entire $1 million" of his net earnings from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour to Palestinian relief organizations, days after he was dropped from the tour over his pro-Palestinian comments.

He also invited New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who said Macklemore wouldn't be welcome at Gillette Stadium for the tour's scheduled performances at the end of September, to match his donation. Within hours, Kraft released a statement saying Sheeran had already asked him to match his $2 million donation to humanitarian aid in the region.

Their statements come amid a growing controversy following Macklemore's removal that has seen all of Sheeran's supporting acts quit the tour. Sheeran is set to play in Philadelphia this weekend.

Sheeran broke his silence about Macklemore's removal from the tour on Tuesday, saying it wasn't his decision but the promoter's. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, Sheeran said.

Here's how the controversy began — and how it continues to unfold.

Earlier this month, Macklemore performed as Sheeran's opening act at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he made pro-Palestinian comments and performed his protest song "Hind's Hall."

The song was written after protests in support of Palestine occurred on college campuses across the U.S. in 2024, and is named after Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed by Israeli troops in Gaza. Israel's military acknowledged in August that its troops had opened fire on the car carrying Hind and her family and said it had opened a criminal investigation into the killing.

"A big part of the ​reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could ​stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free ‌Palestine,'" ⁠Macklemore said onstage earlier this month.

His comments drew criticism from pro-Israel groups including the Israeli-American Council, which started a petition to have the Grammy-winning artist dropped from the tour.

Macklemore was scheduled to perform at eight of Sheeran's 10 remaining shows on the Loop Tour, with Philadelphia being the next stop. After that, Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass., is scheduled for performances on Sept. 25 and 26.

In a lengthy social media post on Monday, Macklemore said, "Ed Sheeran and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop Tour." He described having difficult conversations with Sheeran, whom he considers "a brother."

Macklemore said Sheeran told him that Kraft, whose Kraft Group owns Gillette Stadium, didn't want Macklemore performing at the stadium over his pro-Palestinian comments. Sheeran also told Macklemore that Kraft had appealed to other stadium owners to issue him an ultimatum: "If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues," according to the post.

Macklemore acknowledged that Sheeran was put in a difficult position.

The promoter, Messina Touring Group, confirmed in a statement to Rolling Stone that Macklemore won't perform on his remaining support dates because multiple venues wouldn't allow concerts to proceed with the rapper on the lineup.

Kraft issued a statement to the media, saying that Gillette Stadium is responsible for providing a welcoming environment for all guests attending events at the venue.

"Based on Macklemore's recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran's shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line," Kraft said in the statement.

"I agree with Macklemore. Too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft added.

As the controversy played out, Sheeran remained publicly silent. On Sept. 15, the pop star released a statement on social media, writing, "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated."

Sheeran then explained that he preferred to remain publicly neutral on political issues and that Macklemore's removal wasn't his decision.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me," he wrote.

"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living," Sheeran wrote.

Sheeran's own backing band, Beoga — which had been performing several songs around the middle of each set — announced on social media that they would be departing the Loop Tour in light of Macklemore's dismissal.

"We believe in dialogue as a means of progressing the plight of the Palestinian people. … We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be."

Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe announced in an Instagram post that he had dropped out as an opener on the tour.

"I don't take the decision lightly. Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this," the Irish musician wrote.

"But as Irish people," Rowe continued, "we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children."

Danish pop band Lukas Graham also announced on Tuesday their withdrawal as a supporting act for Sheeran's tour.

Singer-songwriter Finneas also announced on Instagram that he was pulling out of the South American portion of the tour. "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," he wrote. "I have decided to withdraw my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people."

As of Wednesday, Graham and Rowe are still listed as special guests on Sheeran's Loop Tour website.

On Wednesday afternoon, the rapper wrote in a post on Instagram, "I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people."

He then encouraged Kraft to match his donation. "Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting."

Macklemore added, "Writing a check is one of the least costly forms of solidarity available to me. I am doing it because I can, and because these organizations are doing the work while much of the world debates it."

Within hours of Macklemore's pledge, Kraft issued his own statement, saying, "I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people. I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting. Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis. Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges.

"In addition, I'd like the people who are speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships."
