These Are the Best Smart Speakers to Buy in 2026
description: If you're in the market for a smart speaker, these are your best bets.
fullText:
Smart speakers are a crucial element of any smart home setup. They serve multiple roles: a speaker to play your music, movies, or podcasts; a smart assistant, to answer your questions (or, most likely, set your timers); and a smart home hub that all of your smart home products connect back to. In all likelihood, your best choice for a smart speaker is going to be based on the smart home platform you gravitate toward, as well as the devices you already own, but the decision can sometimes be a bit more complex than that.

The best smart speaker for most people is the speaker that most people can use. By that, I mean the device should be broadly accessible and not platform-specific. You should be able to buy the speaker and integrate it directly into your home, regardless of your existing devices or subscriptions. To that point, Amazon's Echo line is the most flexible choice. And among Amazon's many Echo devices, the Echo Dot Max is the best bang for your buck.

The Echo Dot Max isn't Amazon's most expensive speaker, nor is it the cheapest. Instead, it's a bit of a middle-ground option that offers the features most people are looking for in a smart speaker without costing too much. As PCMag notes in its review, the Echo Dot Max can "fill a modestly sized room with sound" and is "nicely balanced," which should be great for casual listening. It might not have the directional audio of Amazon's more powerful speakers, however, so if you're looking for stereo sound or something that delivers more "oomph," you may want to upgrade.

The Echo Dot Max should match most tech needs. Because this is an Amazon product, it has Alexa built in—including Amazon's Alexa+ AI assistant. It supports Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3, and LE Audio. It also supports several smart platforms, including Matter, Thread, and Zigbee, and comes with smart sensors, such as temperature, ultrasonic, wifi radar, and ambient light. That's part of why this is my top pick: No matter what devices or services you already use, you'll be able to use the Echo Dot Max without issue. You could have a Windows PC, an iPhone, Spotfiy, and a variety of smart home devices, and they should all be able to work with the Echo Dot Max.

If you're a dedicated Google Home user, the company's "Google Home" speaker is likely your best bet. Google refreshed its smart speaker this year, the company's first smart speaker since the Nest Mini back in 2019, and it shows: The speaker looks a bit more modern, like a combination of the Nest Mini and a HomePod Mini—which isn't a bad thing at all.

As this is a Google product released in 2026, the Google Home speaker is all about Gemini. That means you can issue Gemini complex, contextual commands, string together multiple requests into one, or make corrections during your request. According to Google, its new assistant is smart enough to interpret these various commands correctly; it encourages users to ask challenging questions based on its accumulated knowledge. For example, you could ask Gemini what the weather is like for your favorite sports team's next game, and it should be able to answer—assuming you've previously clued it in to what team you follow. That said, you'll have to pay Google's subscription to access Gemini's best features, which diminishes those perks a bit.

Leaving AI, as this is a Google Home speaker, it works best with Google Home smart devices. Reviews say it's easy to set up in existing Google homes, and the Google Home app works well. If you have Google Home Premium you can take advantage of features like asking Gemini to review camera footage ("what happened to this vase that broke while I was away?"). You can also pair the Google Home speaker to other Nest speakers, as well as a Google TV.

It isn't just Google Home that makes this speaker worth considering. Reviews say the Google Home speaker sounds great, even with its smaller 58mm internal driver, with improved bass and overall audio quality when compared to the Nest Mini. In fact, CNET says it has the "best audio for a $100 speaker," so it may be a good choice even for users who aren't dead set on Google Home or Gemini—though those users will be the ones to get the most out of this speaker.

Apple users will not be disappointed by an Amazon Echo. But if you're truly embedded within the Apple ecosystem (e.g., iPhone, Mac, Apple TV, Apple Music, etc.), a HomePod mini is the choice for you. This is the only smart speaker on the market that natively works with Siri (with the exception of the much more expensive Denon Home 150), and while that might not entice users who have had poor experiences with Apple's assistant, it does mean it will work across your various Apple devices.

When properly set up, you can use your HomePod mini to add items to your grocery list in Reminders, iMessage friends, locate items in Find My, and, of course, control smart home devices through the Home app. The HomePod mini can also recognize up to six different family members' voices, so Siri can distinguish between who is speaking. And, if you buy more than one HomePod mini, you can use the intercom function to broadcast a message to all HomePods at once.

The HomePod mini works best with Apple's devices and platforms. That means it's easy to connect to an Apple TV (and, if you have two, you can link them together into a stereo pair). It's also designed for Apple Music: You can ask Siri to play something from the service or your library, or, if you have a song playing on your iPhone, you can hold it near the speaker to transfer the track to the HomePod.

Apple says the HomePod mini uses "computational audio" to simulate the experience of a larger, more powerful speaker. While it might not quite trick you into thinking it's something it's not, I can attest that the sound quality is excellent, especially for a speaker this size. It gets plenty loud with great separation between the high and mid frequencies and the bass. It's not the cheapest mini speaker on the market, but it is Apple's cheapest. The company's flagship HomePod is almost triple the price, but it does come with quite a bit more power that may appeal to Apple fans.

Most smart speakers are designed to stay put, but the Sonos Move 2 is meant to be taken with you. This battery-powered speaker has an IP56 rating against dust and water, which means you shouldn't be afraid to take it out to the beach, lake, park, or anywhere with less-than-ideal conditions.

This is a Sonos product, so it's not a surprise to learn that the Move 2 has excellent sound quality. PCMag says Sonos' portable speaker "produces powerful stereo sound" with a "pleasing mix of sculpted lows and highs." This speaker has dual left- and right-channel tweeters to produce that stereo audio, with the ability to get loud should you want it—though PCMag notes that you can achieve a full and deep bass even at a moderate volume.

The Move 2 supports Sonos Voice Control, but also Alexa, making it a bit more versatile than some other platform-specific options on this list. This speaker also supports Wi-Fi 6 and Apple AirPlay 2, though it's stuck on Bluetooth 5.0, which is a bit of an outdated version. Really, the biggest disadvantage here is the price tag. This is the most expensive speaker on this list by far, and unless you really need Alexa or Sonos Voice Control features, you might be better off with a high-quality Bluetooth speaker. Still, this is about as good as it gets for portable smart audio.

title: 10 Hacks Every Audible User Should Know
description: Use these tips and tricks to get the most out of Amazon's audiobook platform.
fullText:
Audible is one of the largest and most popular audiobook services out there, and with good reason, as it gives you access to a huge library at a competitive price. Unlike Libby—which is also an excellent audiobook platform—you don't have to sit on a wait list for popular titles, and purchases are (mostly) yours to keep. These are the tricks you need to know to get the most out of Audible and save some money along the way.

If you like to have the option to either read or listen to your books, you can take advantage of Kindle and Audible crossovers to get the audio version of certain titles for free, or at least less than what you'd pay if you bought them outright on Audible. One option is to add audio upgrades to your purchased Kindle books: you can see which books are eligible and how much the narration add-ons cost using the Matchmaker tool. If you have a Kindle Unlimited subscription, you can also get lots of Prime Reading books with Audible Narration at no additional cost. Finally, when adding a Kindle book to your cart, look for the Add audiobook checkbox to see how much the companion Audible version costs—in some cases, it may be cheaper to purchase the bundle than to use an Audible credit or buy them separately.

For users on Audible's monthly subscription plans, credits are use it or lose it—if you cancel, your unused credits expire even though you've already paid for them. If you fall behind on your listening or forgot that you've been paying for Audible and want to catch up, you can temporarily pause your membership instead of canceling. This way, you retain your credits without being charged the ongoing fee. You can pause your membership for up to 90 days every 12 months. In the app, go to Profile > Membership > Manage > Pause Membership.

If you threaten to cancel your Audible subscription, Amazon may try to keep you by giving you a discount on your membership or applying a free credit to your account. This one isn't a guarantee, but users report that the cancellation flow frequently includes retention offers. There's no harm in trying, and you don't have to confirm the cancellation if there's no incentive. On the Audible web interface, tap your name > Membership Details > Cancel membership. Note that if your subscription is billed through Apple or Google, you have to cancel through the App Store or Google Play Store and may not receive a retention offer.

With Audible's standard monthly billing plan—priced at $8.99—you get a credit added to your account each month and listening access for as long as you maintain your membership. If you cancel, you lose unused credits and your existing library. A premium subscription billed monthly at $14.95 lets you keep books purchased with credits even if you cancel, though unused credits will expire immediately. But if you This plan is also about $2.50 cheaper per credit than a monthly premium subscription, and you get access to additional sales and discounts.

If you try to share a single Audible account with multiple users, you won't be able to listen to the same book at the same time without disrupting each other's progress. But you can share purchased titles with other members of your Amazon Family account, which allows keeps individual progress and listening histories separate. An Amazon Family can include two adults and up to four children. Note that you can't share unused credits—only purchased books.

The default skip forward and back times in Audible are 30 seconds, but you can customize these intervals to as little as 10 seconds and as long as 90 seconds. If you frequently find yourself rewinding, especially when listening to dense material, you may want to shorten the interval so you don't have to go back and listen to a longer segment each time you need to repeat a sentence. Note that back and forward can be set at different lengths. Go to Profile > Settings > Player > App display > Back 30s Forward 30s to change the skip times.

Audible's Clip feature saves short segments from your books to reference later. You can also add notes to clips so you don't have to keep a separate document or write down start/end times for snippets. Tap +Clip on the title's player screen to automatically save a 30-second segment, then click Edit on the confirmation banner and use the sliders to mark the exact beginning and end points and enter notes. To play a saved audio clip, open the title's player screen, tap the Clips & Notes button, and identify the clip you want to listen to. You can either play just the clip or start listening again from the clip.

If you're waiting for audiobooks to go on sale before you buy them, add titles to your wish list to see deals and discounts at a glance all in one place. You can use the list to regularly check for price updates, and Audible may also send email or push notifications when titles you've saved are on sale. In the Audible app, tap Add to Wish List on the title's detail page, and then view your list via Library > Lists > Wish List.

Audible has a fairly generous return policy, so if you don't like a book or a narrator, you can get your credit back to use on a different title. You must be a Premium subscriber to take advantage of returns, and only audiobooks bought with credits (versus cash) are eligible within 365 days of purchase. Note that you may lose this privilege if you abuse it, so you probably shouldn't listen to every title all the way through and then try to return it. Also, always listen to the book sample if available to make sure you don't hate the narrator.

If you purchase titles on Audible, you'd expect that the files are yours to keep—just like a physical book—but this isn't a guarantee. Third-party platforms like Libation and OpenAudible allow you to download, back up, and convert your audiobook files so you can store and listen to them locally. Libation is free and open source but some users note that it's a bit more technical. OpenAudible has some free functionality, but you'll have to buy either an annual or lifetime subscription to get access to file conversion and other premium features.

title: 'Let's go, let's go' - inside catastrophic derby VAR mistake
description: The controversy surrounding the VAR decision to allow Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby has rumbled on for days, so what led to the error?
fullText:
"Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!"

The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby.

No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors the Premier League has seen.

Donohue and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, inexplicably failed to notice that Enzo Fernandez was three yards offside before he tried to head the ball.

The goal was given, and Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0.

Refereeing has always been a goldfish bowl of scrutiny and pressure, heightened by the introduction of VAR.

The Premier League made a "more efficient application of VAR to reduce delays" one of its football principles for the season.

Has the game tried to prioritise speed over accuracy?

The urgency in Donohue's voice was all too apparent.

"Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go!"

It was a panicked exchange between the VAR and the replay operator. Not calm, collected and methodical. Rushed and chaotic. The opposite of how a video official should operate.

Officials hear repeatedly - from fans, pundits, radio phone-ins and newspaper columns - that VAR has to be quicker. That delays are not acceptable.

In the Premier League stakeholders' survey - which includes managers, coaches and supporters - the key theme for improvements to VAR was the speed of decisions.

This has to create pressure - but it is no excuse for such an error.

City boss Enzo Maresca had some sympathy speaking on Wednesday, though he was of course the beneficiary of the gaffe.

"To make a decision in 10, 20 seconds is not easy for them," said Maresca.

"Sometimes they make mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes. It's part of our job."

Referees' chief Howard Webb has taken the desire for quicker reviews on board, but it is still a balancing act.

There has been a positive impact, as far as the stats go.

VAR delays - including the referee making an announcement to the crowd - have been reduced, from an average of 46 seconds per game to 36 seconds season-on-season.

Yet the only other VAR mistake, the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, also arguably came about because the incident was cleared too quickly.

Completing a VAR review in the shortest possible time is not about skipping steps. And it was a critical mistake by Donohue and Antrobus.

Speed is a factor, but the most serious error in process came before Donohue tried to rush through the attacking phase.

Donohue asked the replay operator to stop the video on the first replay when Josko Gvardiol touched the ball to cross into the area. He then went immediately into the semi-automated offside technology.

The VAR team should have assessed the full picture, from the playing of the cross to the head of Haaland. This would have provided awareness of Fernandez's position and impact.

They did not, and the events inside the penalty area were not considered until the attacking phase was looked at.

Donohue has received much of the criticism, but arguably Antrobus' involvement, or lack of, was just as influential.

The AVAR's contribution to the entire review was to utter "no, yeah" about the potential touch by Fernandez. This was one second before Donohue uttered the words "final decision is goal, check complete".

Antrobus' role is to provide the checks and balances, to make sure the VAR has not missed anything. This fell short.

There has been only one lengthy VAR delay this season, in the game between Brentford and Sunderland. A Dan Ballard goal was ruled out for a subjective offside against Kevin Danso.

Antrobus was the AVAR in this game, too. There was a great deal of criticism in some parts of the media for that delay, which took over four minutes.

Could that have played on Antrobus' mind on Sunday? We cannot know for sure.

Ironically, Antrobus played a crucial role in steering VAR Tim Wood to the correct offside decision against Danso.

There is also the role of the support VAR, who sits in the operations room next to the match hub at Stockley Park and can intervene on points on protocol.

Aware of what was unfolding with the review, no action was taken.

It would still have been salvageable in the period between the goal being scored and the kick-off.

Maresca criticises focus on controversial winner

VAR did not even consider if Fernandez was offside - Webb

Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible.

But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure.

There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition.

Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials.

All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League.

One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time.

Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer.

Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. It shows how difficult the role is.

The only two VARs to have a clear record over the last two seasons are Nick Hopton and Neil Davies, both graduates from the same accelerated programme.

Persuading referees to hang up their whistles and spend their professional lives in the VAR room is not easy, nor does it guarantee success.

Lee Mason and Mike Dean, the Premier League's only full-time VARs appointed after retirement, were both dismissed by Webb just a few months into his tenure because of a catalogue of errors.

One of the only leagues which has a full team of officials who only act as VARs and never go out on the pitch is Spain's La Liga and second division - yet one glance at the headlines there will tell you the controversy is no different to that in England.

At the start of last season the VAR completely missed that a player who scored a goal was in an offside position when the ball was played.

Pro Ref will have questions to answer over its processes and why a VAR is rushing so desperately over a review in one of the biggest games of the season.

That did not happen when West Ham's stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal was ruled out last season. It took over four minutes - but the VAR came to the correct outcome.

The obsession with speed threatens to undermine all the work behind the scenes.

But that feels like a football problem and not one caused solely by the actions of the VAR.

title: De la Fuente extends Spain contract to 2032
description: World Cup-winning head coach Luis de la Fuente agrees a contract extension with Spain until 2032.
fullText:
World Cup-winning head coach Luis de la Fuente has agreed a contract extension with Spain until 2032.

The 65-year-old's previous deal was due to expire in 2028.

De la Fuente, who guided Spain to their fourth European Championship title in 2024 before securing global honours this summer, is now set to remain in charge for Spain's World Cup defence on home soil in 2030.

Spain will co-host the 24th edition of the men's World Cup alongside Portugal and Morocco, with a handful of matches scheduled for Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay as part of the competition's 100th anniversary celebrations.

De la Fuente succeeded Luis Enrique as head coach in December 2022, following Spain's last-16 exit at that year's World Cup.

Since then, they have lost just twice in 41 competitive matches and won three trophies, including the 2022-23 Uefa Nations League. They finished as runners-up to Portugal in 2024-25.

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time to lift their second men's World Cup crown in July, having defeated England 2-1 in the European showpiece two years earlier.

"His results speak for themselves, as does his work," said RFEF president Rafael Louzan, speaking at Wednesday's World Football Summit in Madrid.

"The public loves and admires him. I offered him an extension because he wasn't among the top 10 in terms of financial conditions. Now he will be.

"We're finalising the agreement so he can remain for several more years. He's been with us 14 years, and I want him to be able to finish his career here."

De la Fuente, who began his coaching career in Spain's lower leagues, spent nine years in Spain's youth set-up prior to replacing Luis Enrique, winning a European Under-19 Championship in 2015, a European Under-21 Championship in 2019 and a silver medal at the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo.

Spain are next in action on 26 September, facing England at Wembley in their 2026-27 Nations League opener.

title: Painful endgame for Gray as stale Hibs slump
description: A club hero, David Gray ends his time as Hibs head coach not to the sound of euphoria from fans, but to the sound of a support collectively exhaling in relief, writes Tom English.
fullText:
It was the strangest kind of farewell; more sadness than satisfaction, more 'thanks for the memories' than 'never darken our door again'.

After a dozen years as a player, a goalscoring and Scottish Cup-winning icon, a coach, an interim manager and, for the last two-and-a-bit seasons, the first team manager, David Gray exited Hibernian on Wednesday evening.

He left, not to the sound of euphoria from the fans, but to the sound of a support collectively exhaling in relief. Given what he did on an immortal day at Hampden in 2016, no Hibs supporter wanted to boo the man they called Sir David Gray, nobody wanted to call for his head. It was a painful endgame, for everybody.

Hibs have sacked many managers in recent seasons, but this was no Nick Montgomery, no Lee Johnson, no Shaun Maloney. Gray was altogether different. Driven, passionate, honest as the day is long, brutally so when talking about how things were going wrong, which he had been doing too much of lately.

Gray's big picture tells us this: he was the first manager at Easter Road to qualify for European football in consecutive seasons since the great Eddie Turnbull in the early 1970s. The kind of slump that Hibs are in right now is entirely in keeping with what's happened at Hibs over the last half century.

He's the only Hibs manager to win at Ibrox in three consecutive seasons. He won at Celtic Park last season, too.

The flipside is also clear. Six successive home defeats in the league equals a grim club record dating back to 1920. Two shots at European Conference League play-offs - and the finance that would have come had they completed the task - were wasted in the most self-harming way.

Six points from six games, ninth in the table, an awful loss to lowly Kilmarnock on Tuesday and a sense of drift did for him. Making the League Cup semi-final, against Hearts, wasn't enough to save him.

Gray sacked by Hibs after six league games

The style of football wasn't easy on the eye, the lack of energy and entertainment was a problem that was only growing. Hibs just look a bit stale, a bit rudderless. Occasionally they can spark into life and show what they are capable of, but those moments have been too fleeting.

Jens Berthel Askou brought zest and enjoyment to Fir Park last season and Alfred Johansson, his successor, is trying to build on that. They both had bad nights on Tuesday but Johansson and Wouter Vrancken at Hearts are attempting to create something compelling and their fans are on board with them all the way.

Maybe Hibs fans want something similar, something shinier, something more exotic. There is the feeling that they have a decent enough squad of players but also a belief that these players should be delivering more than they are.

If there was a table for under-performance, Hibs would be challenging at the top.

Some of those same players must shoulder a chunk of the blame for Gray's demise, but they are a largely protected species, even if a number of them, weak-willed and unreliable, have no right to be protected. You can't sack a dressing room in one day, though. A manager and his assistants? Now that's different.

Gray goes but others must look in the mirror; the players, a sporting director in Malky Mackay, a chairman in Ian Gordon, a chief executive in Dan Barnett who could scarcely be more low-key if he lived in a bunker under Easter Road.

Gordon, presumably, will lead the search for another manager. It would be interesting to do a poll on the level of trust fans have in him and others to land the right man.

Gray took them to third in the league in his first season and fifth last season. There is an argument to be made that on the back of those bottom lines he deserved more time, but he hasn't got it.

He had a tumultuous beginning as Hibs manager; one league win in his first 14 games. In November he was bottom of the league. Hearts were second bottom. More than once Gray seemed to be in trouble only to pull out a series of wins that made him safe.

That first season was a prime example. From bottom of the table, he got them to third by the end. It was a fine achievement. Fifth last season was reasonable, but it must have felt nightmarish to Hibs fans as Hearts roared on and threatened to win the league.

The rise of Hearts adds significant pressure on whoever's managing Hibs. It's just the way it is.

Throughout his time, Hibs had a ruinous capacity to concede late goals that checked momentum and made the search for the holy grail of consistency all the harder.

In 2024-25 Hibs conceded late goals that cost them points against Kilmarnock, Ross County, Hearts, Dundee twice and Dundee United twice in minutes 88, 90, 90, 90, 86, 90, 87 and 90.

Last season that unfortunate habit of caving late on continued too often. They conceded damaging goals against Midtjylland, Legia Warsaw, Livingston, Dunfermline, Dundee and Hearts three times in minutes 119, 90, 98, 90, 90, 90, 88, 90 and 86.

This season they lost to Motherwell in the 85th minute and shipped goals in the 84th and 90th minute against Gent to exit the Conference League.

They salvaged a point, or three, on other days, but they were on the wrong side of the ledger on so many occasions. Gray will have regrets about that. What-might-have-beens. Plenty of 'if onlys' mark his time in the job. His players have cause for reflection, too.

They have no shortage of decent-to-good players at Hibs, but there is something missing, some steel, perhaps, some mentality, some leadership, some coaching nous.

Gray did his utmost to improve things. He always struck you as a manager who lived and breathed the job, who was terribly cut up by it when it didn't go to plan.

Most sacked managers think they could have improved things if they were given time. The betting is that Gray is one of those. He was in trouble in his first season and he found a way out of it to finish in a lofty position. He'd have backed himself to do the same in the months ahead, but that chance has gone now.

Hibs are back at the drawing board. Consistency there, at least. Meanwhile, Gray will start again somewhere else, hopefully strengthened by the experience of how brutal football management can be at times.

title: League Two Fleetwood host Arsenal in EFL Cup - full fourth-round draw
description: League Two side Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the EFL Cup.
fullText:
League Two Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

The Lancashire side reached this stage for the first time in their history with a 1-0 win over Sheffield United on Wednesday night.

And their reward was a plum home tie against Mikel Arteta's men, who beat Ipswich Town 4-2 on Tuesday.

Holders Manchester City will welcome Brighton to Etihad Stadium if they beat Norwich in Thursday's remaining tie, while Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso will visit his former side Liverpool after the Premier League rivals were drawn together.

League One sides Bradford and Peterborough will play for a place in the quarter-finals after they defeated Leyton Orient and Barnsley respectively in the third round.

The remaining fixtures are all Premier League affairs with Fulham hosting Crystal Palace, Bournemouth at home to Aston Villa, Brentford travelling to Sunderland and Everton welcoming Newcastle United

The fourth round will take place during the week commencing 26 October.

title: Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure - but should he be after this latest mess?
description: Manager Michael Carrick insists he does not feel under pressure after Manchester United's EFL Cup exit.
fullText:
Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead.

That is the context to the shocking Carabao Cup third-round exit his old club suffered against Brighton on Wednesday.

It is a period of time that encompasses the legendary Scot's dynasties at Aberdeen as well as United. The Class of '92 were in nappies when John Pratt scored the winner for Tottenham on 4 September 1976.

After holding protests inside and outside the ground before Sunday's loss to 10-man Manchester City, United supporters made their feelings known about their latest embarrassment in three ways.

Most fans simply left as the players embarked on their post-match lap of appreciation.

Some of those who remained booed, as they had done when their side fell behind 21 minutes from time.

It is not certain where 15-year-old JJ Gabriel was while all this was taking place, but nothing happened that would make him think he had got it wrong by turning his back on the club.

Indeed, it is quite possible, probable indeed, that the promised senior debut would have been scrapped given the game situation - and the fact skipper Bruno Fernandes was among the experienced players introduced in the frantic final stages.

"Of course we can turn it around, we have got some really good players," said Carrick. "It feels bad because we haven't had a great week or two, or three weeks."

Man Utd lose to Brighton from 2-0 up to end 50-year record

What next for Gabriel and Man Utd?

'Let's go, let's go' - inside catastrophic derby VAR mistake

Carrick's side have won twice this season, against newly promoted Ipswich at home after falling behind, and Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. They have now lost on three occasions, more defeats than he experienced in 17 matches after replacing Ruben Amorim in January.

He has been around Manchester United long enough to know the pressure losing runs can build.

"I don't feel under pressure," he said. "Either way, that doesn't bother me one bit.

"I understand what goes on outside and how the world works, but it doesn't bother me. What bothers me is winning games, having a good feeling around the place and a good feeling around the group to know we're moving in a good direction."

The problem is it doesn't feel as though they are moving in a good direction. There were certainly not many positives to take from this mess.

The obvious one was Shea Lacey, who marked his first senior start with a well-taken eighth-minute goal. It meant he became the first teenager to score on his first United start since Marcus Rashford in February 2016.

Lacey was one of eight changes made by Carrick. Defensively, those changes were not a success.

Diogo Dalot was one of the three players to keep their place. His form has deserted him. Noussair Mazraoui is the back-up left-back, which only heightens the debate over the wisdom not to buy one before the transfer window closed. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven looked like the inexperienced defenders they are. In midfield Manchester United were overrun.

Yet again, Rashford threatened without managing a goal or an assist. He came closest to levelling when he sped beyond the Brighton defence, but his shot was saved by Jason Steele.

"The longer the game went, the more we had control," was the concise assessment of Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler. "I thought we deserved to win."

Carrick didn't dispute the assessment.

His greatest sadness was for Lacey, who should have had his name in lights but instead was part of a team scuttling off the pitch to the sound of boos and harsher criticism.

"It's a shame that Shea's moment, such a great moment for him, for his family, his friends and the whole academy; to have an academy player come in and have a moment like that, gets a bit lost, unfortunately," said Carrick.

"It won't for him when things settle down but, as we sit here now, it feels that it was a long time ago."

Carrick also addressed the JJ Gabriel situation.

"He's a young boy, he's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players, their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure, we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation," he explained.

But ultimately, for any manager, the assessment of their work comes through results.

"Being here toughens you up over a period of time," he said. "It depends how you deal with it. You've got to deal with it in a way where you can cope with it and you can bring out the best in yourself. However you do that, with your motivation and the confidence deep within yourself to know we can win football matches.

"We've gone out of the cup tonight, and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that. I'm honest enough to say that's how it feels. But it doesn't have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction."

Manchester United have one more game before the international break, at Fulham on Sunday.

For the general wellbeing of the club, Carrick's team really need to win.

Speaking on Sky Sports, former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said he wasn't sure they will.

"Right now, they're miles off it," he said. "It doesn't matter how good the manager is, if you don't have the right players it makes it really difficult.

"There's a reason why the other managers have struggled. Sooner or later the pressure's always going to come on.

"This weekend becomes a huge game. He doesn't need another poor result, otherwise all of a sudden you're going into the international break and everyone's talking about you. The winners tonight are the players who didn't play."

title: Boehly and Walter sell Chelsea stakes to Clearlake
description: Clearlake Capital acquires full control of Chelsea as chairman Todd Boehly, director Mark Walter and Hansjorg Wyss sell their stakes in the club.
fullText:
Chelsea chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter have sold their stakes in the club to majority owner Clearlake Capital.

Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss has also sold his stake, meaning Clearlake - led by co-founders Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano - have now acquired full control of the club.

Boehly, Walter and Wyss each had a 12.8% stake, with Clearlake previously owning 61.5% of the Blues.

American Boehly will leave his role as chairman, a position he has held since 2022, when the consortium bought the club for £2.3bn from Roman Abramovich, who was sanctioned by the UK government in March 2022 over alleged links to Russian president Vladimir Putin - something he has denied.

BBC Sport reported in August that Boehly and Walter were exploring selling their stakes.

Multiple sources said talks started within Chelsea's ownership group after a rift, first apparent in 2024, led both sides to explore buying each other out.

Boehly, who is a co-owner of baseball franchise the Los Angeles Dodgers, said it had been an "honour" to serve as Chelsea chairman.

"I would like to thank the many who helped secure a bright future for the club, including the English Premier League, the coaches and players, the talented leadership and staff at Chelsea, and the legions of dedicated fans," he added.

"I have valued my partnership with Clearlake and the wider ownership group, and the collective decisions and investment we have made to support the immediate and long-term success of the club. I am confident that Chelsea is well positioned for continued success under Clearlake's leadership."

Since the takeover in 2022, Chelsea's highest Premier League finish is fourth in 2024-25, with the club also winning the Uefa Conference League and Fifa Club World Cup that season.

The club have also had a remarkably high turnover of players over the past four years, with the initial strategy focusing on signing young players to long-term contracts.

Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League last season and appointed Xabi Alonso as their manager in the summer.

Eghbali and Feliciano thanked Boehly for his "time and contribution" as chairman, saying he will "always be a part of the Chelsea story and family".

They added their focus is to "continue investing in the club's infrastructure, sporting performance, player development and delivering long-term success for Chelsea and the club's supporters".

Chelsea have ongoing plans either to redevelop Stamford Bridge or move to a new stadium, which sources say had created tension at times between Boehly's camp and Clearlake.

A club statement said there will be "no changes to the day-to-day operations, leadership or strategy at the club" as a result of Clearlake assuming full control.

Walter, the co-owner and chief executive of global finance firm Guggenheim Partners, where Boehly also began his financial career, last month sold the Los Angeles Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.23bn) - a year after buying a majority stake in the NBA franchise.

Separately, US federal prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating companies in Walter's business empire.
